questions.context: R49-52: narration 'measures in the POV's own units', with exact figures from 'a trained eye, an instrument, or the notes'; seconds and minutes are free (R51-07); travel runs in miles (R53-08). The archive measures in feet, yards, miles and stone, beside in-world units such as a fire's length (Kharven) and the ikke, one turn of a process (Dawi); SI is the metric system.

options.label: The POV's own units
options.consequence: Current law. A Kharven guard counts in bowshots and a pot's boil, a Measurewright in yards, pounds and joules. Units characterise, and the exact figure stays with trained eyes.
options.sample: The standpipe stood two bowshots past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked out to it in the time a pot takes to boil and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, cast iron the size of a man's head, a thing two riders had grunted to lift. The needle took a long breath to move.

options.label: Imperial for everyone
options.consequence: Miles, yards, pounds, stone and hours in all narration, with EU and AU/s (Essence Units, and Aether Units per second) for any practitioner. Victorian and familiar; local units fade to flavour in mouths.
options.sample: The standpipe stood four hundred yards past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked out to it in six minutes and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, eight stone of cast iron that two riders had grunted to lift. The needle took a full second to move.

options.label: Metric and SI
options.consequence: Metres, kilograms and joules in all narration, the science and LitRPG default and easy to compare across books. Least period-sounding; the Victorian look must carry the period alone.
options.sample: The standpipe stood three hundred and sixty metres past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked out to it in six minutes and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, fifty kilograms of cast iron that two riders had grunted to lift. The needle took a full second to move.

options.label: Imperial street, SI instruments
options.consequence: Narration measures in Imperial units; instruments, Measurewrights and Guild papers read in metres and joules, as Victorian science did. Two systems on the page, and the gap marks who is trained.
options.sample: The standpipe stood four hundred yards past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked out to it in six minutes and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, eight stone of cast iron that two riders had grunted to lift. Her dial was lettered in metres and joules, the Guild's measure. The needle took a full second to move.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps units as characterisation, gives the trained eye the crisp figures LitRPG readers want, and leaves the north and the East their own measures.

questions.title: Numbers: words or digits
questions.question: In narration, are numbers spelled out or written as digits?
questions.context: No rule sets it: the archive spells numbers out almost everywhere and keeps system figures such as '3,332 EU' in the author notes, with a few in prose. Book style (the Chicago Manual, a standard style guide) spells out up to one hundred; LitRPG prints digits. Readouts are the LitRPG section's, and rung numerals are LR5's.

options.label: Words always
options.consequence: Every number in narration spelled out, however large; digits only in documents, instruments and notes. Literary and period; a big exact figure runs long on the page.
options.sample: The quartermaster walked the stack twice and wrote nothing until the second pass. The stack came to four hundred and twelve rounds, split. Thirty-one sacks of salt stood against the wall, two of them wet through. He did the sum on the board with his thumbnail: forty-six days at the ration, or a hundred and nine at the ration they would all be on by the Thin Weeks.

options.label: Small in words, big digits
options.consequence: Words up to one hundred and for round numbers; digits for exact large counts and every system figure (Level, EU, AU/s). Sourced figures stand out as data.
options.sample: The quartermaster walked the stack twice and wrote nothing until the second pass. The stack came to 412 rounds, split. Thirty-one sacks of salt stood against the wall, two of them wet through. He did the sum on the board with his thumbnail: forty-six days at the ration, or 109 at the ration they would all be on by the Thin Weeks.

options.label: Digits for every measure
options.consequence: Digits for every count, measure and system figure; words only for rough numbers (a dozen, a few hundred). Crunchy and scannable, LitRPG-style; the prose starts to read like a report.
options.sample: The quartermaster walked the stack twice and wrote nothing until the second pass. The stack came to 412 rounds, split. 31 sacks of salt stood against the wall, 2 of them wet through. He did the sum on the board with his thumbnail: 46 days at the ration, or 109 at the ration they would all be on by the Thin Weeks.

questions.rec_reason: The prose stays literary, and wherever a sourced system figure appears it reads as hard data, the LitRPG pleasure without turning narration into a report.

questions.title: Capitals for system terms
questions.question: Which system terms take a capital letter in narration?
questions.context: The archive capitalises Wellspring, Essence, Aether, Stage and Level, and writes reserve and the draw lower case. Canonical terms are 'used exactly, no approximation' (R14-5-CANONICAL_TERMS), and Check 37 is meant to validate Wellspring and Family names (R18-7-CHECK37); verify.py runs neither. LitRPG capitalises every system noun; literary fantasy capitalises proper names only.

options.label: Canonical terms capitalised
options.consequence: The archive's habit fixed as a list: Stage, Band, Grade, Level, Wellspring, Essence, Aether, Pressure and Sub-Stat names capitalised; reserve and the draw lower case. Plain senses (a band of riders) need care.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's Pressure reached the desk. That put him well past Murmuring. The coil on the counter gave his Band and his Grade before he had his gloves off, and his Level after that, the needle settling by hairs. He had taken the draw at a Wellspring that morning; the Essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

options.label: Proper names only
options.consequence: Named Stages, named Wellsprings, Archons and Sub-Stat names capitalised; common system nouns lower case (stage, band, grade, level, wellspring, essence). A calmer literary page; a checker must tell term from word by context.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's pressure reached the desk. That put him well past Murmuring. The coil on the counter gave his band and his grade before he had his gloves off, and his level after that, the needle settling by hairs. He had taken the draw at a wellspring that morning; the essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

options.label: Caps follow the POV
options.consequence: A Guild or practitioner POV capitalises system terms; a commoner's narration lowers them and reaches for folk words, because to him they are plain words. Uneven across a book by design. The sample is the gate-boy's POV.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's weight reached the desk, the push the old men called a stage. The brass coil on the counter twitched and settled, and the clerk wrote band, grade and level, words the gate-boy knew the way he knew the names of far cities. The man had been at a wellspring that morning; the essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

options.label: Full LitRPG capitals
options.consequence: Every system-touched noun capitalised: Reserve, the Draw, the Main, Breakthrough, Traits, Paths. Strongest game feel and easiest to scan; heavy on the eye, and a capital no longer marks a name.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's Pressure reached the desk. That put him well past Murmuring. The Holding Coil gave his Band and his Grade before he had his gloves off, then his Level, then his Reserve, the needle settling by hairs. He had taken the Draw at a Wellspring that morning; the Essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

questions.rec_reason: It is the house habit already, gives the system a visible LitRPG surface without capitalising every noun, and yields a fixed list a checker can hold.

questions.title: New words: what kind, how many
questions.question: When a scene needs a word for something new, which kind of coinage does it reach for, and how many may one scene carry?
questions.context: R51-14: 'No ceiling on WOTR terms per page'; a mid-scene coinage is logged and becomes canon only if Isaac reuses it (R50-28). WOTR coins three ways: English compounds (night-stone, draw-hum), native words (kiilut, tallut) and capitalised labels. A portmanteau fuses two words into one, as smog fuses smoke and fog.

options.label: All three, by owner
options.consequence: English compounds for common things, a culture's native word where that culture owns the thing, capitalised labels for system and instrument things; no cap, all logged (R50-28). The blend in one rule.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once and left the main-quiet behind it. In the Moto lane they called it shizumari and put up their shutters. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. On the gauge-housing the needle lay against CUTOFF, and across the river the rich side kept its lights.

options.label: English compounds, sparing
options.consequence: Old-English-style compounds and the odd portmanteau first (night-stone, main-quiet), two or three new words a scene at most, each placed so context carries it. Amends R51-14; less strangeness per page.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once and the main-quiet came down on the street. Kettles stopped ticking. Dogs lifted their heads. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. On the gauge-housing the needle lay flat, and across the river the rich side kept its lights.

options.label: Native words, freely
options.consequence: Each culture's own tongue first, as many words as the scene's cultures supply: Moto, Dawi and Kharven words for new things. Strongest culture and Eastern flavour; the heaviest reading load.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once. The Moto lane said shizumari and put up its shutters, and the Dawi cooper at the end of the row cut a tallut on his door-post for the hour. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. Across the river the rich side kept its lights.

options.label: Plain capitalised labels
options.consequence: New things get plain English names with a capital, LitRPG-style: Cutoff, Draw Rate, Main Silence. Instantly clear and game-flavoured; little poetry in the coinages.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once and the street went into Cutoff, the Board's word, painted on every gauge-housing in the quarter. Kettles stopped ticking. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. Across the river the rich side kept its lights, its Draw Rate a copper dearer on the bill.

questions.rec_reason: Each tradition coins its own way, compounds for the West, native words for the East and labels for the game layer, and giving each its own territory blends them without a muddle.

questions.title: A word bank per culture
questions.question: Does each culture get a written word bank, the way it already has a senses bank?
questions.context: Each Standing Inventory carries senses, objects, oaths and proverbs, and scenes 'draw from it first' (R51-31). Native words sit scattered: Kharven kiilut and hulluk among the swears, Dawi tallut (the entry) and kaas (the cask) among the objects. A word bank lists a culture's own words and trade terms with meaning and speaker; DS6 asks the other new fields.

options.label: A Words entry everywhere
options.consequence: Every Inventory gains a Words entry: native words, trade terms, slang and address forms, each with meaning and who says it. Scenes draw from it first; a checker can spell-check against it.
options.sample: Dawi, Words. tallut: the entry in the Tally. kaas: the cask. thrus: the cut rune. nikkat: the angle-set. ikke: one turn of a process. Speaker for each: any Dawi. In a scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart, and told the Accord quartermaster the brew wanted one more ikke.

options.label: Only cultures with tongues
options.consequence: Banks for cultures that keep their own language (Kharven, Dawi, Moto, Elven, the Korean and Chinese strata); English-speaking cultures keep trade slang under Objects and Exchange. Less to build; Accord slang stays unlisted.
options.sample: Dawi, Words: tallut, kaas, thrus, nikkat, ikke, each with meaning and speaker, as for every culture that keeps its own tongue. Accord: no Words entry; its trade terms stay under Objects and Exchange (the cut plate, mine scrip, the split tally). In a scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart. The quartermaster paid in mine scrip.

options.label: One shared lexicon
options.consequence: One WOTR lexicon file, every culture's words in one list tagged by culture and linked from each Inventory. One place to check spelling and collisions (R51-11); scenes filter it by culture.
options.sample: WOTR Lexicon, one file. hulluk (Kharven): wet wood, the older word. kaas (Dawi): the cask. kiilut (Kharven): one of the dead left without the Waiting. tallut (Dawi): the entry in the Tally. Each Inventory links to its own rows. In a scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart.

options.label: No bank, by ear
options.consequence: Words borrowed or coined in the scene and logged (R50-28), with no standing list. Freest drafting; spellings drift, and a checker has nothing to hold.
options.sample: No standing list. Scene log, the Seat cellars: tallut and kaas, already in the Dawi Inventory; keg-quiet, coined this scene, canon if Isaac reuses it. In the scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart, and the cellar went keg-quiet while he counted.

questions.rec_reason: A bank per culture keeps Eastern and Northern words consistent from scene to scene and gives the checker a list to hold, the way the senses bank already works.

questions.title: Real-language swears in narration
questions.question: May close-POV narration curse in a real Eastern language, and whose POV may do it?
questions.context: Close-POV narration may carry 'timeless profanities plus swears invented deliberately for WOTR' (R51-02), each culture's own first (R51-29); neither says in which language. Real swears: Japanese kuso (shit), Korean jenjang (damn it), Chinese tamade (damn it; Lu Xun wrote an essay on it in 1925). English and WOTR swears stay whatever is chosen.

options.label: English and WOTR only
options.consequence: R51-02 read narrowly: English hard words and WOTR-invented swears (Kharven canon, the other cultures' drafted sets once approved, R51-35). Real Eastern words stay out of the POV's head.
options.sample: His heel went on the yard ice and the rest of him followed. He landed on the dispatch case, ribs first. Shit. He lay there a breath with the cold coming up through his coat, then got a thumb to the seal. Whole. Frozen piss, but it was whole, and the ribs would tell him about it by morning.

options.label: The POV's own tongue
options.consequence: A Japonic, Korean or Chinese-stratum POV may think his own language's swears, romanised, correct and never italic (R50-01, R50-32), beside English and WOTR ones.
options.sample: His heel went on the yard ice and the rest of him followed. He landed on the dispatch case, ribs first. Kuso. He lay there a breath with the cold coming up through his coat, then got a thumb to the seal. Whole. Kuso, but it was whole, and the ribs would tell him about it by morning.

options.label: Borrowed across cultures
options.consequence: Any POV may curse in a language he has lived among, the way soldiers pick up each other's swears: a Hallenfeld courier who rode with Moto riders thinks kuso. Each word still correct.
options.sample: His heel went on the yard ice and the rest of him followed. He landed on the dispatch case, ribs first. Kuso, the one Moto word he had kept from the riders. He lay there a breath with the cold coming up through his coat, then got a thumb to the seal. Whole. Shit, but it was whole, and the ribs would tell him about it by morning.

questions.rec_reason: An Eastern POV gets real heat in his own tongue while each culture's own swears still come first, which is the blend in a single word.

questions.title: The hard-ban list
questions.question: Which stock-phrase families join the hard-ban list, and should any current item be trimmed?
questions.context: R51-10's fifteen hard-ban items FAIL at first use in narration and speech. Speech formulas such as 'you court death' are DL2's, so new families bind narration only. Pick none to keep the list as it is; each sample shows a flagged line, then the same beat clean.

options.label: Cultivation-translation stock
options.consequence: Bans 'qi surged', 'a cold glint flashed', 'sucked in a cold breath' and 'killing intent surged' in narration. The Eastern feel comes from method, never from translated filler.
options.sample: Flagged: The elder sucked in a cold breath, and a cold glint flashed in his eyes. Clean: The elder set his cup down without looking at it. Tea ran over the lip and along the table, and he let it run. His eyes stayed on the boy's feet, where the floorboards had split along the grain.

options.label: Western fantasy stock
options.consequence: Bans 'the steel sang', 'a grim smile', 'his blood ran cold', 'every fibre of his being' and 'darkness gathered'. Grimdark's own worn phrasing goes out with the imported kind.
options.sample: Flagged: A grim smile touched the elder's lips, and the boy's blood ran cold. Clean: The elder set his cup down without looking at it. Tea ran over the lip and along the table, and he let it run. His eyes stayed on the boy's feet, where the floorboards had split along the grain.

options.label: LitRPG stock
options.consequence: Bans 'power surged through him', 'stronger than ever', 'a wave of power' and 'his stats soared'. Growth shows in the body and on the instrument.
options.sample: Flagged: Power surged through the boy, and he was stronger than ever. Clean: The boy's hands had stopped shaking. Under him the floorboards had split along the grain, and across the hall the elder set his cup down without looking at it and let the tea run.

options.label: Trim the false hits
options.consequence: Narrows three items to their stock sense: a will called a testament passes, 'visceral' passes in anatomy (the visceral pleura, R49-45), 'orbs' passes for lamps and regalia. The stock senses still fail.
options.sample: Flagged today: The elder set his cup down on his testament, sealed that morning in grey wax, and let the tea run along the table. After the trim the same line passes, since a testament here is a will; the stock sense still fails.

questions.rec_reason: A blend imports each tradition's filler along with its strengths, so banning all three families keeps the borrowing at the level of method, and the trim stops the list catching honest words.

questions.title: What the checker enforces
questions.question: Which vocabulary checks does verify_scene gain?
questions.context: verify_scene (build/verify.py, the house prose checker) FAILs the hard-ban list and WARNs on modern words in narration, Earth calendar words and holy swears. Spelling, loanwords, italics, capitals and number style go unchecked; wotr_terms.txt, the canonical list Pack Fourteen calls for (R14-5-BUILD_TERMS_LIST), was never built. A FAIL blocks a Natalie reply; a WARN asks for a read.

options.label: Word-bank spelling check
options.consequence: Native words are matched against the culture banks (VB10); a near-miss FAILs as a misspelt Wellspring does (R14-5-NEAR_MISS_FAIL); unknown words are listed for the scene log (R50-28).
options.sample:
FAIL near-miss: "kilut" in "...he would have been kilut, and every woman..." (bank: kiilut, Kharven; R14-5-NEAR_MISS_FAIL)
info words in no bank: main-quiet, shizumari (log with the scene, R50-28)

options.label: Canonical term list
options.consequence: wotr_terms.txt is built from Fracture of Worlds, the glossary and the Codex; Stage, Band, Wellspring and Family names are checked for spelling and capitals (VB8), and a near-miss FAILs (R14-5-NEAR_MISS_FAIL, Check 37).
options.sample:
FAIL near-miss: "Murmering" (canonical: Murmuring, a Stage; R14-5-NEAR_MISS_FAIL)
WARN capitals: "his band" where Band is a system term (VB8)

options.label: New ban families FAIL
options.consequence: The families chosen in VB12 FAIL at first use in narration, as R51-10 does; looser variants of a banned phrase WARN for a read.
options.sample:
FAIL hard-ban phrase: "a cold glint flashed" in "...breath, and a cold glint flashed in his eyes..." (cultivation family, VB12)
WARN stock watch: "a grim little smile" (Western family; keep only if it is the POV's own idiom)

options.label: Style-sheet warnings
options.consequence: WARNs for the house style set here: an italicised loanword (VB2), a digit where words are due (VB7), an archaic word outside its culture's dial (VB4). Holds the style without blocking a reply.
options.sample:
WARN italic loanword: "*kiilut*" (R49-49-FOREIGN)
WARN number style: "31 sacks" (words up to one hundred, VB7)
WARN archaic word in a plain-dial scene: "ere" (Kharven dial, VB4)

questions.rec_reason: Each check holds one of this section's choices in place mechanically, so the blend's vocabulary survives long sessions instead of drifting back to defaults.

sections.title: Interiority
sections.intro: What the POV thinks and feels on the page. Current law runs deep: running interiority, frequent italic thought, and emotion shown in the body first, then named in the POV's own word.

questions.title: Modern idiom in thought
questions.question: May a POV's thought carry modern idiom that narration may not?
questions.context: R48-13 keeps modern words to speech ('narration keeps a timeless register'), and verify warns on them in italic thought too; this reopens it for thought, ruled 2026-09-26. Korean web-novel and LitRPG (game-stat fiction) heroes think in a running, joking modern idiom; Lord of the Mysteries' hero, a modern man reborn, keeps his modern asides. Gamer words (build, dump stat) are asked in the LR section.

options.label: Timeless thought (current)
options.consequence: R48-13 holds for thought: italic thought keeps narration's timeless register, and verify keeps warning on modern words in italics.
options.sample: The journeyman sat on the cold step of the Sum-gol station with the season's drill-list on his knee and argued with himself. *Tempering, again. The master says Tempering, and the master has outlived three men who drilled their hands instead.* His hands were good. Everyone said so. *Good hands and a short wind. That is how the river took Jae-won.* He crossed out the hand-drills one by one, slowly, as if each line cost him something he would have to find again in the spring.

options.label: Thought as he speaks
options.consequence: Italic thought may use whatever the POV would say aloud, modern words included; plain narration stays timeless. verify drops italic thought from the modern-word check.
options.sample: The journeyman sat on the cold step of the Sum-gol station with the drill-list on his knee. *Right. Tempering, again. The master's whole philosophy is don't die, which, fine, hard to argue with from a man who's buried three students.* His hands were good; everyone said so. *Good hands, no wind. Great combination. That's how the river got Jae-won. Okay.* He crossed out the hand-drills one by one and tasted every line of it in his teeth.

options.label: Close narration too
options.consequence: In a close register, narration fused with the POV's idiom may carry his modern words as well; medium and distant registers stay timeless. R48-13 is amended for close POVs.
options.sample: The journeyman sat on the cold step of the Sum-gol station with the drill-list on his knee. Tempering, again. The master's whole philosophy came down to don't die, which, fine, was hard to argue with from a man who'd buried three students. His hands were good, everyone said so, and good hands with no wind were a great way to end up like Jae-won, face down in the river with an excellent grip on nothing. He crossed out the hand-drills one by one. Okay. Tempering it was.

questions.rec_reason: It gives the web-novel and LitRPG inner voice to the POVs who would talk that way, while narration keeps the timeless register R48-13 protects.

questions.title: How reasoning shows
questions.question: Which ways of showing a POV's reasoning should join running interiority, with each register choosing among them?
questions.context: R48-39 (ruled 2026-09-26) makes interiority 'deep and running'; this only adds modes beside it. Lord of the Mysteries (a Chinese web novel) has its hero plan in explicit steps and risk lists; LitRPG heroes reason from figures like a puzzle; Kawabata stops thought short of its point and lets an image carry it. The approved Moto register already leans toward the unsaid.

options.label: Stepwise lists
options.consequence: A reasoning POV may set thinking out as numbered steps, risk lists or tests in italic thought; R16-8-CHECK33's cap on technical terms in italics eases.
options.sample:
The scout said the Keld had moved their camp off the north road. Lorn laid it out while the man drank.
*One. Moved camps mean moved herds, and there has been no moss on that road since the grass.
Two. So somebody moved the herds for them, or bought them.
Three. Or he is saying what he was paid to say.
Test: the boots.*
Good boots. Better than a scout's pay. *Three, then, until it isn't.* He poured the man a second cup and said nothing yet.

options.label: The unsaid
options.consequence: Thought may stop short of its conclusion and leave an action or an image to carry it, as Kawabata does; deep interiority becomes one mode of two, chosen per register.
options.sample: The scout said the Keld had moved their camp off the north road. Lorn let him drink. Outside, an axe was splitting rounds for the woodpile, and the halves knocked onto the stack, one, then the other. Lorn looked at the scout's boots for some time. They were very good boots, Stannvaard-welted, oiled that week. He poured the man a second cup, and moved the jug a little nearer to himself.

options.label: Reasoning from figures
options.consequence: A POV who can read rank or price may reason from readings and figures as evidence, as LitRPG heroes do; every figure still traces to a source (R12-5).
options.sample: The scout said the Keld had moved their camp off the north road. Lorn did the sum while the man drank. The token at the scout's throat was a Murmuring disc, Seat-stamped, and a Murmuring scout drew a scout's pay. The boots on him were Stannvaard-welted, a season's wage at the least. *Pay, less boots, leaves a man somebody gave boots to.* He poured the scout a second cup and said nothing yet.

questions.rec_reason: Each belongs to one strand (Lord of the Mysteries' planner, Kawabata's restraint, LitRPG's figures), and letting the POV's register choose among them and running reasoning keeps every head distinct.

questions.title: Carrying feeling
questions.question: How should feeling be carried on the page?
questions.context: R49-07: 'show it in the body first; the POV may then name it in his own word'; this reopens it, ruled 2026-09-26. Japanese mono no aware (the gentle sadness of passing things) and Korean han (grief held for years without release) are carried by held images and seldom named; the Icelandic sagas show feeling only in deeds; LitRPG names states plainly.

options.label: Body, then named (current)
options.consequence: R49-07 stands: the body first, then the POV's own word if he has one.
options.sample: The old woman sat the Waiting for her son in the unheated death-house with her hands in her lap, and by the second night her knuckles had locked and she could not open them. She did not try. Near dawn she found the word for the thing under her breastbone. Rage, she thought, and was surprised by it. At the wall, at the cold, at the boy for going up the north stair when he had been told twice. She sat with it until the light came.

options.label: Held image, never named
options.consequence: In chosen scenes the feeling is never named and one held, concrete image carries it, as mono no aware and han do; R49-07 gains a register-level exception, and the image obeys R5-C2.
options.sample: The old woman sat the Waiting for her son in the unheated death-house with her hands in her lap, and by the second night her knuckles had locked. Frost stood on the stone under the bier. Through the door she could see his woodpile across the yard, split to the height of her shoulder and no higher, the axe still sunk in the last round where he had left it for the morning. Snow was filling the cut around the blade. She sat until the light came.

options.label: Deeds only, saga-style
options.consequence: Feeling appears only as deed and terse speech, as the Icelandic sagas show it; interiority falls silent at grief and shock.
options.sample: The old woman sat the Waiting for her son in the death-house. On the second night her knuckles locked. She left them locked. On the third morning she went out to his woodpile, worked the axe free of the last round where he had sunk it, and split the rest of the stack herself before noon, every round, without stopping to eat. Then she gave the first bowl to the neighbour's boy, as is done. The elder asked how she did. The stack was full, she said.

options.label: Named plainly
options.consequence: Narration may name the state outright, before or without the body, as LitRPG does; verify's named-emotion warning is retired.
options.sample: The old woman sat the Waiting for her son in the unheated death-house, and she was grieving, and she was angry, and under both she was afraid of the spring, when the ground would thaw and there would be no reason left to sit. By the second night her knuckles had locked. She knew all three feelings by name, had known them since the first hour, and the names did nothing about the cold. She sat until the light came.

questions.rec_reason: It is the Eastern contribution the archive lacks, grief carried by a thing left unsaid, which WOTR's Gone lists and R5-C2's elegy-on-a-concrete-thing already point toward, and it enters as an extra mode inside current law.

sections.title: What description covers
sections.intro: Today's law sets how dense description runs and almost nothing about how wide it ranges, so the page keeps returning to bodies, rooms, papers and wounds. These questions decide whether range becomes law, which thin subjects it pushes, and whose eye picks them out.

questions.title: How wide description must range
questions.question: Should the range of subjects a scene describes become law, and in what shape?
questions.context: R48-02 asks 'Lush throughout' and R51-31 sends scenes to the sense bank first; nothing sets range, and the archive leans on bodies, rooms, documents and wounds. Chinese and Japanese prose rotate landscape, season and household; the Victorian novel ranges over money, streets and institutions; LitRPG describes gear, loot and monsters.

options.label: Range by ear (current)
options.consequence: No range rule. Lush density (R48-02) and the sense bank first (R51-31) stand, and Natalie widens by judgement. Nothing new is checked.
options.sample: The quartermaster's store smelled of seal fat and wet felt. Hob Varley stamped the snow off his boots and waited. The man behind the trestle was finishing a count and did not look up for it: broad, grey at the temples, his knuckles split by the cold and greased against it. A blubber lamp spat on the shelf over his head. Even indoors his breath stood white. "Courier," he said at last. "How's your stack?" Hob had no stack. He had a satchel of Hallenfeld paper and two feet he could no longer feel.

options.label: Lead plus two, thread-checked
options.consequence: Each scene brief names one lead subject group and two supporting ones, the lead rotating scene to scene; session end flags any rotation group untouched for six scenes.
options.sample: Salt bought a bench and broth at the quartermaster's store, and Hob Varley had brought Accord silver, which nobody north of the arrays would take. A carter let him have one gritty bar for two marks. Twice its price. He paid. Outside the door a boy was splitting rounds for the woodpile, setting each on the block with its checks toward him so the axe found the crack and the halves fell clean. Over the grey rock of the Seat the aurora had come up green. The quartermaster scraped the bar with a thumbnail to see it was salt all through, and let him in.

options.label: Five groups every scene
options.consequence: Every scene or full turn touches at least five subject groups, one of them from the rotation list. The widest page, with some risk of reading as a survey.
options.sample: Snow came sideways off the rock as Hob Varley reached the outer town. Over the Seat the aurora stood in two green folds. Six hundred men were breathing in the yard, and a woman ladled broth; the first bowl went to an old rider whose hands had gone in the Thin Weeks, and she held it to his mouth herself. A boy split rounds. He stacked them pale ends outward. At the store the quartermaster took Hob's salt, scraped it with a thumbnail and gave him a bench. On a nail above it hung a child's sling of plaited horsehair.

options.label: Thread count only
options.consequence: Scenes stay free. Session end lists every rotation group untouched for six scenes, and the next scene brief must draw on them.
options.sample: Hob Varley came in along the horse lines, where the Seat kept its riding stock under hide awnings. Steppe horses, shaggy for the winter. Frost in their manes. A grey mare stood hipshot with her eyes half shut and one ear turned to him, and dung steamed in the cold behind her. Where the wind had scoured the rock bare, moss showed black. It was the only growing thing for a day's ride, and when the clans said "when the grass comes," this was what came. The store stood at the end of the lines. The seal fat reached him before he found the door.

questions.rec_reason: It turns your ask into something a brief can carry: one subject the scene is built around, two at its edges, and a thread check so nothing goes dark for long. A floor of five per scene reads like a survey.

questions.title: The land and what lives on it
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation the range rule pulls from?
questions.context: Heavy groups (bodies, interiors, documents, wounds, machinery) need no push; the rotation lists the thin ones. No Inventory has a land, sky, plant or animal field, plants come up about 0.5 times per 1,000 words, and the moon never reaches the page. Chinese shanshui (mountain-and-water painting) and Japanese season poetry put this group first; Tolkien walks the road.

options.label: Land, water and sky
options.consequence: Terrain and ground underfoot, rivers, sea and shore, the long view, and the night sky (Shiro, the five wanderers, the Nail, the aurora) join the rotation.

options.label: Seasons and weather
options.consequence: Thaw, rain, heat, fog and each culture's signs of the turning year join the rotation, beyond R53-09's actual weather in every outdoor scene.

options.label: Plants and animals
options.consequence: Trees, crops, herbs, blossom, birds, insects, working beasts, and Well-spawn looked at as creatures join the rotation.

options.label: History in layers
options.consequence: Ruins, re-used stone, a road laid over an older road, and heirlooms with their makers join the rotation, beside the Gone lists (R53-31).

questions.rec_reason: These three are the first subjects of the Eastern half and the thinnest in the archive. History already reaches the page through the Gone lists (R53-31) and elegy, so it needs no rotation slot.

questions.title: The public world
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation the range rule pulls from?
questions.context: Interiors run heavy; architecture as style, dress after first sight, streets and crowds run thin (crowds about 0.3 per 1,000 words). R59-07 and R59-08 set the Victorian city and class-layered dress. Dickens reads a city whole; the Japanese war tale reads rank in armour lacing; cultivation novels (Chinese fiction of climbing toward immortality) make a sect's grounds display its power.

options.label: Architecture as style
options.consequence: Buildings are described for style and ornament as well as use and wear; the Moto 'one thing made that serves no function' finally gets looked at.

options.label: Dress and adornment
options.consequence: Cloth, cut, colour by rank, wear and repair, jewellery, cosmetics and worn scent join the rotation, past the first-sight inventory.

options.label: Streets, markets, crowds
options.consequence: Squares, alleys, hawkers, stalls and haggling, arcades and branded goods (R60-07), and the crowd as one body join the rotation.

options.label: Power on show
options.consequence: Processions and entrances, seating by precedence, courts and punishments (R53-11), Guild halls and academy grounds as displays of standing, and ranking boards join the rotation.

questions.rec_reason: Dress and streets are where class shows without a word, and power on show is common ground for Martin's courts, the cultivation sect and the LitRPG ranking board.

questions.title: Home, table, rite and play
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation the range rule pulls from?
questions.context: No festival has reached the page, no instrument, game or toy is attested for any culture, and children and the rich are nearly absent. R59-15 licenses theatre, music hall, sport and fairs. Pansori (Korean sung storytelling), the court arts of The Tale of Genji and the great household of Dream of the Red Chamber (classic Japanese and Chinese novels) make this group a world's texture.

options.label: Households, young and old
options.consequence: Servants and the order of a house, the rich at home as well as the poor, the child's games and chores, and old age at the fire join the rotation.

options.label: Food and taste
options.consequence: Ingredients, cooking, street food, drink, hunger and rationing, and taste in the mouth join the rotation. How a meal is written is DS8.

options.label: Rites and festivals
options.consequence: Rites performed on the page, household observance, funerals and mourning, festivals, and folk taboos acted on join the rotation.

options.label: Music, art and play
options.consequence: Instruments and songs, carving and painting, theatre and storytellers, games of chance and skill, sport and toys join the rotation.

questions.rec_reason: A world with no song, no game and no festival reads as all work and grief, and grimdark lands harder once the reader has seen what there was to lose.

questions.title: Culture-keyed noticing
questions.question: Should a culture decide what a description notices, and whose culture: the viewer's, the place's, or both?
questions.context: No rule keys what a POV notices to culture; R48-04 keys only metaphor, to 'the POV's own life'. Tanizaki (Japanese novelist, In Praise of Shadows) reads a room through shadow and lacquer; the Victorian novel reads one through price. The Inventories already imply each eye: Moto accuracy, Accord weight and seal, Kharven scarcity.

options.label: Plain sensory eye (current)
options.consequence: Rooms are described through the senses and the sense bank; only metaphor is keyed, to the POV's own life (R48-04). No culture decides what gets noticed.
options.sample: The hall was cold and dim, and Tobias Kell stood where the steward had left him while his eyes caught up. Lamps burned low along the walls. Bare stone underfoot, swept. At the far end a dais held a low table and nothing else. Somewhere behind a screen a man was cutting at wood with a small knife: a scratch, a pause, a scratch. The steward came back. He bowed from the waist and said the lord would see Kell after the bread.

options.label: The viewer's culture decides
options.consequence: The POV notices what his culture's eye catches wherever he stands: an Accord clerk prices a Moto hall, a Kharven rider counts its fuel. Each Inventory gains a 'Notices first' line.
options.sample: Tobias Kell priced the hall before his eyes had finished adjusting. There was no meter by the door. So the lamps burned oil, and dear oil by the smell, the kind an Accord house would have metered and billed by the quarter. The lacquer on the dais was a clerk's wages for a year. No board hung anywhere. There was no seal and no register in sight, and that troubled him more than the cold, because nothing said in a room with nothing written in it would ever be entered. The steward bowed and told him to wait for the bread.

options.label: The place's culture decides
options.consequence: A place is described through the eye of the culture that built it, whoever enters: a Moto hall reads through shadow, lacquer and silence. Each Inventory gains a 'Notices first' line.
options.sample: The hall kept its light low on purpose. Lacquer on the dais was a red so dark it read black until a lamp guttered, and then a seam of garnet ran along the edge and went out. Fourteen scratches stood in the doorpost at hand height. The oldest were worn smooth by thumbs. The floor had been swept twice. In a niche sat one carved bird that served no purpose Tobias Kell could find, and the steward, bowing once from the waist with nothing moving but the cloth of his sleeves, left him a silence to fill.

options.label: Place supplies, viewer judges
options.consequence: The place's Inventory sets what is in the room; the POV's culture sets what he makes of it, misreadings included. Each Inventory gains a 'Notices first' line for both jobs.
options.sample: Lacquer on the dais was a red so dark it read black until a lamp guttered, and Tobias Kell's first thought was what it had cost. Fourteen scratches stood in the doorpost at hand height. A tally of debts, he decided, and looked along the walls for the register that matched it. There was none. In a niche sat one carved bird doing nothing at all, which any Accord house would long since have sold. The steward bowed and left him a silence. Kell filled it by counting the lamps.

questions.rec_reason: The place supplies the subjects and the outsider supplies the misreading, so one pass characterises both cultures, and the folk error stays uncorrected as R53-15 wants.

questions.title: New Standing Inventory fields
questions.question: Which new fields should every Standing Inventory gain, so description has something to draw on across the range?
questions.context: R6-8 set nine categories (food, greeting, oaths, time, the dead, objects, exchange, proverbs, body); later rulings added senses, Gone, folk beliefs and literacy. Nothing supplies land, building, dress, living things, music or law, though R60-21 sets succession 'on its Inventory'. New fields are looked up from the wiki (R53-29), each culture's when it next reaches the page.

options.label: Land, sky, living things
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains terrain and climate, the sky by its own names, seasons and their signs, and what grows, is kept, hunted and feared; Temperature joins the senses entry.

options.label: Building, dress, the street
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains architecture and ornament, the house plan, dress by rank (cloth, cut, colour, adornment, worn scent), and its market and street.

options.label: Music, play, festivals
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains instruments and songs, games and toys, and one or two festivals written as performed: who does what, and in what order.

options.label: Law, succession, roads
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains law and punishment (R53-11), succession (R60-21), and roads, vehicles and inns.

questions.rec_reason: Range needs supply: without these fields every culture keeps being described through what it eats, swears and owns. Drafting each culture's fields when it next appears spreads the cost.

questions.title: Craft and labour on the page
questions.question: When a craft or trade is on the page, how much of the work itself gets described?
questions.context: R6-5 keeps 'The rust described in full' and R12-6 gives a rite 'an order of operations', but the archive names crafts more than it shows them and never looks at finished work for its quality. O'Brian's sea novels and the Japanese master-craftsman story give work step by step; wabi-sabi (the beauty of the worn and imperfect) looks at what it made; LitRPG crafting gives recipe and grade.

options.label: Named when used (current)
options.consequence: Crafts appear when the plot uses them and pass in a line or two. Nothing new is required.
options.sample: The carver cut the ward into the new doorpost while the courier watered his horse, and by the time the horse had drunk it was done. The groove showed nothing. Ketsuen wards never do. He wiped sap off the chisel on his thigh, tapped the post once with the mallet handle and listened, head on one side. Then he nodded. The courier paid him in dried fish and rode on before the light went.

options.label: Shown as process
options.consequence: Whenever a craft is on the page, at least one stretch runs as process: tool, material and steps in order, with the worker's body doing them.
options.sample: The carver laid his palm flat on the cedar and left it there until the sap under the bark stopped feeling cold. Then the awl. He scored the outline shallow, along the grain. The chisel went in at the top of each stroke and came out at the bottom, three passes to a stroke, each deeper than the last, and he blew the chips clear between them. Sap rose in the cut. He let it rise. When the last groove was done he tapped the post with the mallet handle and listened to the note it gave back.

options.label: Process and its beauty
options.consequence: Process as in B, and the finished thing is looked at for its quality: what good work looks like in that craft, through the POV's eye.
options.sample: He scored the outline with an awl and cut each stroke in three passes, blowing the chips clear. Then he stepped back. The courier understood at last why people walked a day to see the old wards at the valley gate: the grooves ran with the grain so cleanly that the glyph might have grown there. Sap welled in the deepest stroke. It hung, amber on pale timber. There was no colour in the ward and no ornament, since a Ketsuen ward shows nothing, and this one showed nothing down to the last hair of the cut.

options.label: Full craft set piece
options.consequence: Once per arc a craft gets a passage at set-piece length: choosing tools, judging material, each step, the risks, the finished thing and its price.
options.sample: He chose the chisel by its handle, the one worn dark where his thumb went, and stropped it on his boot. Then the awl. Then a pot of lamp-black for the line, because his teacher had never let him trust the eye on green timber. The cedar had to be wet enough to take a clean groove and dry enough not to tear. He pressed a thumbnail into the post. Too warm. He sat down on his kit to wait for the sun to come off the wood, since a ward cut in a warm post wanders, and the station paid a meal and a dry bed either way.

questions.rec_reason: It fills the gap the archive shows most clearly, the beauty of finished work, where the Japanese and Western craft traditions meet; a full set piece stays available whenever a craft is the plot.

questions.title: The table
questions.question: When a meal is on the page, what of it gets described?
questions.context: Food is named in the archive and rarely tasted (about 1.5 mentions per 1,000 words), and table customs appear as a line. Dream of the Red Chamber spends pages on dishes and seating; Martin lists a feast course by course; Japanese prose gives a small portion and its vessel full attention. WOTR tables already carry laws: the skin at a Kharven door, the Moto host's three days.

options.label: Named, as now
options.consequence: Meals and customs appear as a line: what was served and who ate first. The archive's current habit.
options.sample: At the door the woman held out the skin and the courier drank, because every Hallenfeld man who rode north was warned what it meant to refuse it. Inside there was broth and windmeat and a place on the bench. He ate what he was given. The old man in the corner had the first bowl. The courier had the third, and was glad of it.

options.label: Tasted in the mouth
options.consequence: Every meal on the page gets taste: what the food does in the mouth, its heat, fat and sourness, how long it chews. The order of serving stays a line.
options.sample: The skin came first, at the door. It was sour and faintly fizzing, and it left a film on his teeth that tasted of yeast and the inside of a seal. Then the broth, with the fat still floating, hot enough to scald the roof of his mouth; he kept drinking. The windmeat was hard as bark. It softened slowly. Salt came out of it, and game, a little at a time and more the longer he chewed.

options.label: Served in its order
options.consequence: The table is shown as a rite: who is served first and by whom, from what vessel, who eats last, and what goes unsaid about it. Taste stays a line.
options.sample: The woman met him on the step with the skin unstoppered and did not move until he had drunk. She took it back without wiping the mouth. Inside, the bowls came off the hearth in their order: the first to her husband's father, whose hands had gone in the Thin Weeks and who was fed by the youngest girl; the second to her husband; the third to the courier. She ate last, standing, from the bottom of the pot. Nobody remarked on it.

options.label: Order and taste both
options.consequence: The order of serving and the taste in the mouth are both on the page whenever a meal is.
options.sample: The woman held the skin out on the step until he drank. Sour, fizzing. It coated his teeth with yeast. Inside, the bowls came off the hearth in their order, and the first went to her husband's father, whose hands had gone in the Thin Weeks, so the youngest girl fed him. The second went to her husband. The third came to the courier: broth with the fat still floating, salt and marrow under the scorch, hot enough to scald. She ate last, standing, from the bottom of the pot.

questions.rec_reason: The order of serving is the cheapest way to show who matters in a house, and taste is the sense the archive uses least; WOTR's tables already have the customs to fill both.

questions.title: Money, price and provenance
questions.question: When money changes hands or a notable object is handled, what of its price, grade and history reaches the prose?
questions.context: R53-17 keeps money before magic and R53-07 has scenes quote the approved price table, yet the archive seldom prices or traces a thing. LR17 asks the set-off item card; this asks the prose. Balzac and Dickens put a price on everything; cultivation novels stage an appraisal; Japanese tea-ware records a famous bowl's owners. Tick none to keep current practice: objects carry what the POV notices.

options.label: Price whenever money moves
options.consequence: Every purchase, wage, fee and bribe on the page names its sum in the culture's money, quoted from the approved price table; north of the arrays, payment in kind is named as exactly.
options.sample: The dealer laid the sword on a fold of green baize. Five gold, he said. The courier had paid eighteen for the horse tied outside and did the sum before he could stop himself: better than a quarter of a horse, for a blade. A trooper's sabre on the rack behind was ticketed at eight silver. North of the arrays nobody would take his gold at all; up there it was salt, a bar to the silver mark and more in a hard winter. He counted out five. He kept his face still.

options.label: Appraisal by a trained eye
options.consequence: A dealer, smith or Measurewright reads grade, maker and age aloud in his trade's words, cultivation's appraisal scene in prose; the POV follows only as far as his own eye. Serves LR17's C.
options.sample: The dealer turned the blade to the lamp so the courier could see the stamp at the ricasso, the Hallenfeld proof-house's mark struck once and clean. "Proofed," he said. "Probatum. Stannvaard steel, by the grain in the flat, and the edge never reground, so whoever carried it never had to lean on it." He sighted down the spine with one eye shut. "Forty years old, near enough. The cord is new." The courier could see the stamp. Everything else the man saw stayed in the man.

options.label: Its life and lineage
options.consequence: A notable object is described through who made, carried, mended and died with it, the way a famous tea bowl keeps its line of owners; Tier and price stay off unless asked.
options.sample: The sword had passed through three pairs of hands before it reached the dealer's baize. A captain of the Hallenfeld road had it made, and his initials were still on the pommel, half worn away by a palm. His son had it reground after a bad notch, and the new bevel caught the lamp a shade brighter than the old one near the guard. The third man rewound the grip in black cord and died of the Thin Weeks with it on his hip. The courier drew it a few inches and felt all three of them in the balance.

questions.rec_reason: Money before magic gets its figure every time coin moves, which costs a clause, and lineage gives notable objects the history a card cannot carry. Appraisal already has its forms in LR8 and LR17; B stays the prose route if LR17 goes to C.

questions.title: Landscape and sky
questions.question: How much of the land and the sky does an outdoor scene describe?
questions.context: R53-09 shows 'the actual weather' in every outdoor scene and R49-22 keeps the world 'described, not personified'; past that, the archive sees land through windows and the sky almost never. Chinese shanshui builds a view in far, middle and near planes with the person small; Tolkien gives the road its miles; canon names Shiro, the five wanderers and the Nail.

options.label: Weather and near ground (current)
options.consequence: The actual weather (R53-09) and the ground near the POV; wider land and sky only when the plot needs them.
options.sample: The snow had stopped by the time they topped the ridge, and the cold came down hard behind it. The scout reined in. Below, the Seat's walls showed darker grey on the grey rock, with lamps in the gatehouse and smoke standing over the outer town. The courier's horse blew and stamped. He had lost the feeling in his face an hour back. "Keep to the ruts," the scout said. "They're frozen hard enough to ring."

options.label: One wide view outdoors
options.consequence: Every outdoor scene gets one wide view built far, middle and near, with the people small in it, and the sky in it after dark.
options.sample: From the ridge the whole north lay open. Far out, the plain ran white and level to a line of low black hills, and over them the aurora hung in two green folds. Nearer, the rock rose grey. The Seat sat on it, its old courses darker than the new stone above. Nearer still, the outer town's stacks put their smoke straight up into the still air. On the ridge two horses stood blowing. The courier, very small against all of it, could not feel his face.

options.label: Land as route
options.consequence: Ground that is travelled is described as route: distance, slope, footing, what the road is made of, and the time it takes at a walk (R53-08 rates).
options.sample: The last nine miles had taken the light. A mile back the road had come off the moss plain onto bare rock, and the ruts there were frozen hard enough to ring under the hooves, so the scout kept to the crown, where the ice lay thinnest. From the ridge it ran downhill all the way. A long slope of wind-scoured stone. The Seat at its foot. Two hours at a walk, the scout said, if the grey held.

options.label: The sky every night
options.consequence: Every night scene names the sky: the moon's phase (Shiro, the Lamp), which wanderers are up, the Nail, the aurora, and what people read in them.
options.sample: The Lamp stood a hand above the black hills, a night past full, and behind the Seat the aurora moved in two green folds without a sound. The Nail held still overhead. Low in the south the Red Ox burned dull. The scout pointed it out with his whip: it was going backwards this season, he said, and nobody sane started anything under it. Under all that light the Seat was a grey rock with a few lamps on it. The courier's breath stood white.

questions.rec_reason: One wide view per outdoor scene is the clearest Eastern gain on the page and fills the thinnest gap; the sky comes into it after dark, and the route stays available whenever the road matters.

questions.title: Bodies after first sight
questions.question: Once a person has had their first-sight inventory, how is their body described when they come back?
questions.context: R49-28 gives everyone 'the full physical inventory all at first sight'; after that the archive's bodies are mostly hands. Abercrombie and Mantel keep a body changing under wear; cultivation novels dwell on a body's beauty; Holmes reads a life off a frame; LitRPG tracks the body as numbers, which the LitRPG section asks. The Ledger carries injury between scenes.

options.label: When the plot needs (current)
options.consequence: After the first-sight inventory, a body comes back on the page only when the action uses it: a hand, a limp, a wound.
options.sample: The horse-master was at the lines again before light, forking hay with his back to the wind. He nodded when the courier came out. "Your grey's lame," he said. "Near fore. Stone bruise, likely." He bent, took the hoof between his knees, and showed the courier the sole, where a dark bloom of blood sat under the horn. "Three days off it," he said. "Four if you want her to carry you home."

options.label: One changed detail each time
options.consequence: Every return of a person carries one detail of what the body has changed since: a new wound, weight, fatigue, cold damage, a missed shave. The Ledger's costs show.
options.sample: The horse-master was at the lines again before light. Something had gone in his back since yesterday; he forked the hay from the hip in short strokes, and straightened in two stages with a hand on the post. Frost had got into the cracks of his knuckles in the night. They had bled and dried black. He had not shaved. "Your grey's lame," he said. "Near fore." When he bent to take the hoof he did it slowly, and breathed out hard through his nose before he looked.

options.label: Beauty dwelt on
options.consequence: Any POV may dwell on a returning body as something to look at, man or woman, young or old, at length, in the terms of his own life.
options.sample: In the blue hour before light the horse-master's face had the colour and grain of old harness, every crease laid down by weather and kept supple with grease. He worked bare-forearmed in the cold. Each time he lifted the fork the long muscle along the bone ran clean under the skin, rope through a greased block. The courier had come out to see to his grey and stood watching longer than he meant to. "Your grey's lame," the horse-master said, without turning. "Near fore."

options.label: The body as record
options.consequence: A returning person's body is read like a document: trade, age, old injuries and habits read off the frame by any POV with the eye for it.
options.sample: By daylight the courier could read the horse-master's life off him. A rider once. The knees were bowed and the inside of each calf worn hairless by the saddle, and thirty winters of forking hay had built the right shoulder higher than the left. Two fingers on the bridle hand had set crooked after some old kick. The frost-scars on both cheeks were waxy white and old, the kind one bad night leaves. "Your grey's lame," he said. "Near fore."

questions.rec_reason: It keeps every body under the Ledger's cost, one changed detail at a time, which is grimdark's strength; beauty and the read-a-life eye stay open to any POV whose life gives him them.

questions.title: Repetition against novelty
questions.question: How should description balance a culture's recurring signature items against new subjects?
questions.context: R6-9 reads 'Identity is repetition. Novelty is its enemy.', R51-31 sends scenes to the sense bank first, and R53-19 asks two signature items per culture per session. The archive shows the cost: repeated key-rings, stained fingers and closing lines. Homeric and pansori refrains make repetition carry identity; web serials and your 'wide variety of things' pull toward the new.

options.label: Recurrence first (current)
options.consequence: Scenes draw on the Inventory and sense bank first, with two signature items per culture per session (R53-19); invention is logged and secondary.
options.sample: The household sat down once the woodpile had been counted and the count called through the door. Somebody asked the courier how his stack was. He had none. They laughed. The night-stone sat warm at the edge of the hearth where the fire had been. The old man said the boy who had gone down the Hallenfeld road was wet wood, and the woman told him to hush. Outside, the Thin Weeks were coming. Everybody said so, and nobody said it twice.

options.label: Recur, and add one
options.consequence: R53-19's two signature items stay; R6-9's 'Novelty is its enemy' is rewritten so every scene also adds one subject the thread has not described, logged as canon (R53-21).
options.sample: The household sat down once the woodpile had been counted and the count called through the door. The night-stone sat warm at the hearth's edge. The two youngest had a game the courier had never seen: five knucklebones from a seal's flipper, tossed and caught on the back of the hand, the loser fetching snow for the pot. The girl won three times running. She made her brother fetch it bare-handed. The old man called him wet wood, and he went anyway.

options.label: Novelty first
options.consequence: The Inventory becomes a floor: Natalie invents texture freely and logs it, the quota drops to one signature item, and R6-9 is struck.
options.sample: The household sat down to a supper the courier had not met before: seal liver sliced thin and eaten frozen, a pinch of salt on each piece. A bone flute lay on the shelf. Three holes. When the old man had eaten he played a tune on it with no ending, round and round, while the girls plaited horsehair into rope for the spring. The dogs had been let in for the night. They lay against the door in a heap, steaming, and nobody counted anything.

options.label: Recur, changed each time
options.consequence: Signature items keep coming back, and each return shows how they have changed since the last: the woodpile lower, the stone cooler, the insult quieter.
options.sample: The woodpile was counted again and the count called through the door. Lower than last night, by more than a night's burning. The night-stone at the hearth's edge was cooler under the woman's palm than it had been yesterday, because they were banking the fire earlier now. The old man called the absent boy wet wood again. More quietly. Nobody mentioned the Thin Weeks. That was new, and the courier had stayed long enough to mark it.

questions.rec_reason: Signature items keep a culture recognisable and the quota stays; each scene also adds one thing nobody has described yet, logged under R53-21, so the world widens as it repeats.

sections.title: How much and where
sections.intro: How much description a page carries, where it sits, who and what gets the full inventory, and how any of it is checked. Live law says lush throughout and a full inventory at first sight; these questions decide whether that holds as the blend widens.

questions.title: Overall density
questions.question: How dense should description run by default?
questions.context: This reopens R48-02 ('Lush throughout'), ruled 2026-09-26. Chinese baimiao (plain line drawing: a subject caught in one or two exact strokes) and Japanese ellipsis run spare; web serials and LitRPG run light and fast; the Victorian novel runs dense. Your new ask is about width, which density alone does not settle.

options.label: Lush throughout (current)
options.consequence: R48-02 stands: full sensory layering in every scene, slower and denser. The blend widens what is described and keeps the amount.
options.sample: The gauge-house at the end of Tallow Row held the smell of lamp oil and brass polish, and under both, damp iron from the standpipe in the corner, which wept a slow bead at its cap. It was the maintenance hour. The district's hum had dropped to the low note it kept while the Board ran its checks. Mary Coyle hung her coat on the peg. Behind the gauge glass the slate still carried yesterday's readings in the inspector's square hand, and the needle sat just off the stop. It was trembling.

options.label: Spare base, lush peaks
options.consequence: R48-02 is rewritten: one exact stroke per beat in talk, travel and routine work; full layering at arrivals that matter, quiet scenes, set pieces and aftermaths.
options.sample: Mary Coyle let herself into the gauge-house at the maintenance hour and hung her coat on the peg. Lamp oil, brass polish. She lit the lamp and read the needle. It sat just off the stop, where it always sat at this hour, and it was trembling, and in nine years she had never once seen it tremble.

options.label: Light, web-serial pace
options.consequence: R48-02 is repealed: one or two details per beat, short paragraphs, the weight carried by action and dialogue, as web serials and LitRPG read.
options.sample: Mary Coyle unlocked the gauge-house a little after three and hung her coat on its peg. Lamp lit. Kettle on. Nine years of this and she could have done it asleep. Then she looked at the needle and stopped with the match still burning in her fingers. It was trembling. "That's wrong," she said, to nobody, and reached for the book.

options.label: Set by the POV's culture
options.consequence: Density follows the POV's culture: Moto and Yukari spare, Accord and Stannvaard dense with figures and seals, Kharven counted. Each Inventory gains a density line.
options.sample: Mary Coyle entered the gauge-house at fourteen counts past the third hour by the wire clock and signed the book under the inspector's seal, green wax, unbroken. Standpipe capped; one bead weeping at the cap. Lamp oil a third down the reservoir. Six readings on the slate from yesterday, each initialled in the square hand. The needle sat just off the stop, correct for the hour. It trembled. She entered that too, with the count, before she let herself think about what it was.

questions.rec_reason: You ruled lush a week ago and the new ask is width. Widening what lush description covers delivers the blend, and the spare Eastern stroke still reaches the page through one-stroke minor people (DD3) and culture-keyed noticing (DS5).

questions.title: Where description sits
questions.question: Where in a scene should the larger descriptive passages sit?
questions.context: Today texture runs through every beat (R53-30) and arrivals open on the senses (R49-25). Modern Western prose weaves; the Victorian novel front-loads the room; Japanese ma (the meaningful pause) and the held moment of wuxia (Chinese martial-hero fiction) pool description in a lull; chanbara (the Japanese sword film) and Gu Long (a terse wuxia novelist) keep it for the aftermath, where LitRPG puts its loot.

options.label: Woven through (current)
options.consequence: Texture runs through every beat (R53-30) and arrivals open on the senses (R49-25). No passage is held back for a pause.
options.sample: The messenger came in with snow still on his shoulders and went to one knee on the swept stone, and the steward let him kneel there while the lamp by the door finished guttering. "The Shirogane envoy turned back at the pass," the messenger said. Melt ran off his collar and dotted the floor. The steward's hand went to his sash and stayed there. Behind the screen the knife that had been cutting at wood all morning stopped. "Turned back," the steward said. "Or was sent back."

options.label: Front-loaded
options.consequence: The place gets its full description at the entrance and threshold; after that the scene runs on action and talk with single details.
options.sample: The audience hall kept its light low: oil lamps along the walls, lacquer on the dais so dark a red it read black, fourteen scratches in the doorpost worn smooth at the bottom, a stone floor swept twice and cold enough to ache through a boot. A knife scratched at wood behind a screen. The messenger came in and knelt. "The Shirogane envoy turned back at the pass." The steward looked at him. "Turned back," he said. "Or was sent back." "I don't know." "Then find out."

options.label: Woven, pooling in lulls
options.consequence: Texture stays woven through every beat; the longer passages are held for pauses, silences and aftermaths, so the news lands bare and the room is seen in the quiet after.
options.sample: The messenger came in with snow on his shoulders, knelt, and said it. "The Shirogane envoy turned back at the pass." Nobody answered him. In the quiet the lamp by the door guttered and steadied, and melt ran off his collar and dotted the swept stone in a line toward the dais. Behind the screen the knife that had been cutting at wood all morning had stopped. The lacquer on the dais held one seam of garnet where the lamp found it. The steward let the silence run until the messenger's knee began to shake. "Turned back," he said. "Or was sent back."

options.label: Held for the aftermath
options.consequence: While the beat runs, description is bare, amending R53-30 for that stretch; when it is over, the scene looks at what is left.
options.sample: The messenger came in, knelt, and said it: the Shirogane envoy had turned back at the pass. The steward asked whether turned or sent. The messenger did not know. He was told to find out, and went. Afterwards the hall kept the marks of it. Melt from his collar lay in a dotted line from the door to the dais. The lamp by the door had guttered out and nobody relit it. Behind the screen the knife had stopped, and the bird it had been making sat half-finished on the bench, one wing still in the wood.

questions.rec_reason: Woven texture keeps the immersion you ruled for, and letting the larger passages pool in pauses and aftermaths gives the page Japanese ma and the wuxia held moment without slowing the action.

questions.title: Who gets the full inventory
questions.question: Which people, places and things get the full first-sight inventory?
questions.context: R49-28 and Table Rule 11 give a person the full inventory (hair by comparison, face, body by area, clothes, marks) at first sight; places, creatures and objects have no such rule. Baimiao catches a minor figure in one stroke; cultivation novels and the gothic give a sect ground or a castle a full entrance; LitRPG gives every monster its entry. Each inventory costs words in a turn.

options.label: People only (current)
options.consequence: Every person gets the full inventory at first sight; places and things get what the scene needs.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat with a brazier in it. The sergeant who stepped out to meet him had hair the grey of old felt, cropped to the skull, and a broad flat face burned dark across the cheekbones by the wind. He was short and heavy through the chest and belly, bandy in the leg: a rider gone to ground. His hide-coat had been patched at both elbows with sealskin and greased black at the cuffs. A frost-scar crossed his nose. He held out a hand.

options.label: People, places, creatures, objects
options.consequence: Every person, place, room, creature and significant object gets a full inventory at first sight, each in one passage.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat two horses wide, the old dark courses at its foot and new grey stone above, an iron grate overhead with its teeth rimed white, a brazier of seal fat smoking in a niche, and a bench worn hollow by sitting. The sergeant who came out of it had hair the grey of old felt, cropped close, and a flat face burned dark across the cheekbones. He was short and heavy. Bandy from the saddle. His hide-coat was patched with sealskin at the elbows, and a frost-scar whitened his nose. He held out his hand for the papers.

options.label: Major full, minor one stroke
options.consequence: Major people keep the full inventory; minor people (a role until they speak twice or matter, R50-27) get one exact stroke. Places stay as now.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat with a brazier in it. A sergeant came out, bandy-legged, a frost-scar white across his nose, and held out his hand for the papers without a word. He read them upside down, which told the courier he could not read at all, and handed them back. "Go up," he said. "Lead the horse. The ruts will break her legs."

options.label: Places full, minors one stroke
options.consequence: Major people, places, rooms, creatures and significant objects get the full inventory; minor people get one exact stroke.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat two horses wide, the old dark courses at its foot and new grey stone above them, an iron grate overhead with its teeth rimed white. A brazier of seal fat smoked in a niche beside a bench worn hollow by forty years of sitting. Smoke had blacked the walls head-high. A sergeant came out. Bandy-legged, a frost-scar white across his nose, he held out his hand for the papers, read them upside down and gave them back.

questions.rec_reason: Places and creatures earn the full entrance the cultivation, gothic and LitRPG traditions give them, and one-stroke minor people end the identity-card sameness the archive shows; major people keep the full inventory.

questions.title: The order of a first inventory
questions.question: In what order should a first-sight inventory of a person run?
questions.context: Table Rule 11 sets the order: hair by comparison, face, body, clothes, marks, then want and voice. The archive runs it the same way every time, so introductions read like identity cards. The Japanese war tale starts a fighter at his armour; cultivation novels and LitRPG start with standing (realm or level); a culture-keyed eye starts where its culture looks.

options.label: Fixed order (current)
options.consequence: Table Rule 11's order stands: hair by comparison, face, body by area, clothes, marks, then want and voice, in one passage.
options.sample: The Reckoner's hair was the flat unlit white of old bone, bound back in one black cord, and her face beneath it was long and narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise, the eyes set deep under a heavy brow. She was tall. Narrow shoulders, a deep chest, hands too large for the arms. Her coat was dark wool, cut close, the cuffs shiny with wear. A callus stood on her right forefinger, yellow and hard. She came in with both hands open.

options.label: The POV's order
options.consequence: The inventory stays one passage at first sight but runs in the order this POV would look: a clerk prices first, a surgeon reads wounds first, a rider looks at hands.
options.sample: He priced her coat before he looked at her face. Dark wool, close-cut, good cloth kept long, the cuffs gone shiny. Then her hands, shown open as she came in. A callus on the right forefinger, yellow and hard where a nib had ridden for thirty years, and no ink anywhere on them, so a careful one. The face came last, because it was worth least to him: long, narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise, under hair the flat white of old bone bound in one black cord.

options.label: Standing first
options.consequence: The inventory opens on standing as the POV reads it (token, seal, bearing, Pressure if a practitioner), then runs the body in Rule 11's order. The cultivation and LitRPG habit, kept in prose.
options.sample: Her standing came into the room ahead of her face. The Reckoner's case rode on its strap at her hip with the seal hung beside it, and the clerks at the long table set down their nibs before she had said a word. Then the hands, shown open. Then the rest. Hair the flat white of old bone, bound in one black cord. A long narrow face, grey-violet as a four-day bruise. Tall, narrow in the shoulder, deep in the chest, her hands too large for her arms.

options.label: Their culture's order
options.consequence: The inventory runs in the order the described person's culture presents itself: Korvaeth hands first, Moto eyes first, Accord token first.
options.sample: Her hands came first, as a Korvaeth's do: shown open at the door, palms out, then turned, to show there was nothing in them and a callus on the right forefinger hard as horn. Then the cord, one black cord binding the flat white hair. Then she stood still and let him look. That was the face, long and narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise. The coat he took in only when she sat: dark wool, close-cut, shiny at the cuffs.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps your full inventory in one passage and ends the identity-card sameness, and the order itself characterises the POV: an Accord clerk prices the coat before he sees the face.

questions.title: Catalogue or telling detail
questions.question: When should description run as a long catalogue, and when as a single telling detail?
questions.context: No rule governs the long list. Homer's catalogue of ships, Malory's arming, the Japanese war tale's armour list, the Chinese fu (a rhapsody listing a palace or park exhaustively) and the LitRPG inventory make length the point; Chekhov and baimiao trust one telling detail. Lambert already falls into inventory under stress (R52-16).

options.label: By ear (current)
options.consequence: No rule; lush layering decides, and lists appear when the moment seems to want one.
options.sample: The rider armed in the yard with the wall above him. He belted the hide-coat tight, pulled the mail over it, and settled the iron cap with its fur lining down over his ears. His breath stood white. Sword on the left hip. Knife at the small of the back. A boy held the horse, and when he was done he grunted, took the reins and swung up, and the frozen ground rang under the hooves as the horse turned.

options.label: Catalogue at set occasions
options.consequence: Arming, feasts, markets, musters, treasuries and loot may run as full catalogues; elsewhere description stays woven. The chain ceiling (R4-14) still holds, so short sentences flank a long list.
