questions.rec_reason: It is how FOW itself writes the ladder, it gives the LitRPG reader a number to hold, and it keeps the names that carry what each Stage means.

questions.title: Figures in plain narration
questions.question: When narration states a figure on its own authority, where must that figure come from?
questions.context: R49-47 (2026-09-26) lets narration state 'stat names, Grades, Stages, eta, EU figures and Guild words on its own authority', and R51-16 frees Sub-Stat names. Still live against them: R49-52 (figures 'from a trained eye, an instrument, or the notes'), R14-4-SUBSTAT_DIAGNOSTIC_ONLY ('Nobody else reaches for them') and NATALIE.md's 'names only in a mouth'. LitRPG narrators quote the sheet freely.

options.label: Fully free
options.consequence: Narration states any figure from the card whenever it likes. R49-52 narrows to speech, R14-4-SUBSTAT retires, and NATALIE.md's Magic Frame and Table Rule 5 are rewritten.
options.sample: Yoko's Harmonics stood at 345 that morning, an A on a Level of 145, and past the instability line. The ears showed it first. They turned to the kettle before the kettle ticked, and to the door a moment before the dog lifted its head from the flags by the woodpile. Ardency and Dominion sat where they always sat, down at C. The hands round the bowl were no stronger than yesterday's. Brida ladled the broth and pushed the first bowl across.

options.label: What the POV knows
options.consequence: Narration states the figures the POV holds: his own last reading, the card he has seen, what he was told. R49-52 governs R49-47; R14-4-SUBSTAT retires; NATALIE.md is rewritten.
options.sample: Brida knew the figures the Seat kept on file, because she had copied them out herself: Level 145, Harmonics an A, a row of B-Grades under it, and Ardency and Dominion down at C. This morning the A had moved. It showed in the ears, which turned to the kettle before the kettle ticked and to the door before the dog lifted its head. By how much, she could not have said. That would wait for the coil.

options.label: Only with a scene source
options.consequence: Names and Grades are free, but an exact figure appears only when something in the scene supplies it: a readout, an instrument, a trained eye. The strictest reading of R49-52.
options.sample: Brida had no tape and needed none to know the Harmonics had moved. It showed in the ears, which turned to the kettle before the kettle ticked and to the door before the dog lifted its head. An A, she would have said, and climbing. The tape, when Yoko pushed it across between the bread and the salt, said 345. Brida read it twice. Then she pushed it back.

questions.rec_reason: Narration reads like LitRPG, figures and all, while every exact figure is one a person in the scene could hold, which keeps the numbers fair and the POV's ignorance real.

questions.title: Growth moments that earn a readout
questions.question: Which moments of growth earn a readout when they happen?
questions.context: Each is a FOW threshold with canon behind it: Levels from XP; Stage only by Catalyst (the Primer: 'Only a Catalyst raises Stage'); Traits; and first contact with a Wellspring current, a one-off Resonant Surge of roughly 500 XP for minor contact at Band I. LitRPG chimes at every level; cultivation novels save the fanfare for a realm breakthrough.

options.label: Level gained
options.consequence: A short readout when a Level lands, with the stat points it brought. The genre's heartbeat, and the most frequent of the four.

options.label: Stage breakthrough
options.consequence: A readout naming the new Stage and its Tier of Standing when the Catalyst completes. The cultivation novel's big moment.

options.label: New Trait
options.consequence: A readout naming the Trait when it registers. Rare, and each one changes what a character can do.

options.label: Wellspring contact
options.consequence: A readout at first contact with a new Wellspring current (FOW's Resonant Surge) and at a harmonisation. Growth tied to a place.

questions.rec_reason: Each is a real FOW threshold with canon figures behind it, so none needs inventing, and LR9's cap keeps the total from turning into wallpaper.

questions.title: In-scene moments that earn a readout
questions.question: Which in-scene moments may carry a readout?
questions.context: R48-16 lets 'anyone with an instrument or trained eye' state figures 'as often as they would'. LitRPG gives heroes appraisal (a skill that shows a target's stats) and shows damage and mana; WOTR keeps wounds in ATLS classes (the trauma-medicine scale of blood loss, Class I to IV) and Pressure as something 'felt as dread' (R53-14).

options.label: Appraisal
options.consequence: Reading a person, beast or item: the Measurewright at the rail, the coil at the counter, a faculty. The genre's appraisal in WOTR's hands.

options.label: A wound
options.consequence: A diagnostic line in a surgeon's terms: the structure struck, the ATLS class, the minutes left. Brida's 'third bowl' as a readout.

options.label: Pressure
options.consequence: A Stage-gap line when Pressure lands, putting a number on what R53-14 makes a dread. Ordinary people still feel it first.

options.label: Essence spent
options.consequence: A reserve line after a working: what was drawn and what is left. R60-03's hard reserve clock made visible.

questions.rec_reason: Appraisal, wounds and reserve are what an instrument or trained eye really measures. Pressure stays in the body, the one thing canon makes felt before it is seen.

questions.title: How many readouts a scene carries
questions.question: How many readouts may one scene or one turn carry?
questions.context: No rule caps them today. Web-serial LitRPG runs several boxes a chapter and draws its commonest complaint, bloat; Cradle shows almost none. R48-20 already gives WOTR a rhythm: the full three-layer account 'at a working's first display and at the finisher; lighter touches between'.

options.label: One per scene
options.consequence: A single readout, saved for the scene's milestone. Readouts stay rare and heavy.

options.label: Display, finisher, aftermath
options.consequence: Up to three per scene, on R48-20's rhythm; a roleplay turn carries two at most, never two in one exchange.

options.label: As an instrument would
options.consequence: No cap: a readout appears whenever a reader in the scene would read, per R48-16. Instrument-heavy scenes carry many.

options.label: Thresholds only
options.consequence: Readouts only at a scene's threshold or after it, never inside the action, as R12-4's document voice already sits.

questions.rec_reason: It borrows a rhythm WOTR already writes by, gives a fight its crunch at the moments that matter, and keeps the box from replacing the body between them.

questions.title: Readouts and the two-voice cap
questions.question: Does a readout count as one of the two explaining voices an engagement may carry?
questions.context: R12-4-VOICE_MIXING_RULE: of the four explaining voices (the POV's read, the knowledgeable second, the opponent, the document), 'Do not run more than two in one engagement.' A LitRPG screen is either a fifth voice or the document voice in a new shape. Figures also let a reader rebuild the call himself, which R13-8 asks of every fight.

options.label: Counts as the document
options.consequence: A readout fills the document slot, so with one on the page only one other voice may explain. Engagements stay lean.

options.label: Outside the cap
options.consequence: A readout states figures and explains nothing, so it never counts; two voices still do the explaining, and the reader checks the call against the figures.

options.label: Cap rises to three
options.consequence: When one voice is a readout, three may run. More crunch, more voices, more words per exchange.

questions.rec_reason: The cap exists to stop over-explaining, and a bare figure explains nothing on its own; outside the cap it keeps R12-4's discipline and gives R13-8 a page the reader can check.

questions.title: Numbers inside a fight
questions.question: What figures may a fight show while it is happening?
questions.context: R60-01: 'most fights end in the first seconds'; R60-03 runs Essence and stamina 'on a hard clock'; a combat turn is six seconds (R47-11); the Stat Ledger sits in the author notes (R14-6-CHECK29). LitRPG logs damage and mana per hit; The King's Avatar, a Chinese pro-gaming novel, has commentators call the play live; Western grimdark shows no figures at all.

options.label: Nothing until after
options.consequence: Current practice: no figures inside a fight. Cost shows in the body, and the Stat Ledger in the notes carries the numbers.
options.sample: The Shirogane man came in high from his guard, and Yoko took the bind on the strong of her blade. His intent reached her nose before her eyes caught up: oil, old sweat, the sour edge of hurry. He meant to wind. She went Indes, in the same instant as his turn, and slid down his steel to the cross until her point rested on his collar. The working behind it was small. It left a thin cold ache under her sternum, and her fingers wanted to shake.

options.label: Grades at the read
options.consequence: The POV's read names Grades and gaps before or between exchanges, as estimates in her own terms; no running figures. The genre's sizing-up without a log.
options.sample: Her nose gave her the read before the bind closed. His Dexterity sat a Grade over hers, an A against her B by the smell of a man whose hands had been fast all his life, and his Harmonics far under. Any exchange that speed decided, she would lose. So she took the bind on the strong of her blade. She went Indes as he began to wind and kept the fight where the steel touched, where his wrists told her what they meant before they did it, until her point rested on his collar.

options.label: A second calls them
options.consequence: A Measurewright or second at the rail reads a gauge aloud between exchanges, so figures arrive in a mouth, as R12-4's knowledgeable second.
options.sample: "Ninety on the draw," said the Measurewright at the rail, reading the yard gauge without looking up, and the Shirogane man came in high from his guard. Yoko took the bind on the strong of her blade, smelled the hurry on him, and went Indes as he began to wind. Her point came off his cross and rested on his collar. "Still ninety," the Measurewright said. "She never pushed it. Stop there." The men along the fence let their breath go.

options.label: Exchange log
options.consequence: Set-off lines per exchange: the action, the draw, the reserve. The full LitRPG combat log, every figure from the card or marked estimate.
options.sample:
The Shirogane man came in high from his guard. Yoko took the bind, smelled the hurry on him, and went Indes as he began to wind.

[Exchange 2 · bind, Indes · draw about 90 AU/s · η 0.60]
[Reserve about 185,000 EU, estimate]

Her point came off his cross and rested on his collar. The cold ache under her sternum arrived a breath after the line, and her fingers wanted to shake.

questions.rec_reason: Grades at the read give a fight its LitRPG sizing-up without running figures the card cannot supply, and R60-01's fights end too fast for a log. Inside a fight this read is LR9's display readout; LR8's reserve line and LR12's number for a cost wait for the finisher or the aftermath. A gauge at the rail (C) still suits sanctioned bouts where one would stand.

questions.title: Body first or number first
questions.question: When a cost or a gain lands, which reaches the page first, the body or the number?
questions.context: R48-37: 'An ability's cost shows in the body: tremor, heat off the skin, thirst, a Crystal ache.' R16-3 wants 'the real mechanism and the system term in the same breath'. Korean System novels put the message first and the body after; Western grimdark keeps the body and drops the number; cultivation novels give both at a breakthrough.

options.label: Body now, number later
options.consequence: The cost lands in the body in the scene; the figure arrives at the next re-assay or in the notes. Grit leads and crunch follows.
options.sample: The fox-fire came up her arms in the dark like a fever looking for a way out. Her knuckles lit cold amber, then her wrists, and the heat came off her in a sheet that dried her lips. Her tail beat once against the bedframe. She held still. She counted breaths until the light sank back under the skin. The figure waited three days for the Measurewright's coil, and when the coil came at last its needle stopped past the red scratch somebody had cut at the instability line.

options.label: Body, then number
options.consequence: The body first and the readout in the same beat, a line after. Both on the page together, with the body always ahead.
options.sample:
The fox-fire came up her arms in the dark like a fever looking for a way out. Her knuckles lit cold amber, then her wrists. Heat came off her in a sheet and dried her lips, and her tail beat once against the bedframe hard enough to shift it on the boards. The line came when the light began to sink.

[Harmonics 345. Past the instability line.]

She held still. She counted breaths until the light was gone from her wrists and the bedframe stopped creaking.

options.label: Number first
options.consequence: The readout lands at the instant of change and the body catches up after it: the System novel's order.
options.sample:
[Harmonics 345. Past the instability line.]

The line came first, cold and exact, and Yoko's body caught up a heartbeat later. The fox-fire came up her arms in the dark and lit her knuckles cold amber, then her wrists. Heat came off her in a sheet that dried her lips. Her tail beat once against the bedframe. She held still. Then she counted breaths, slowly, until the light sank back under the skin and the room was only dark again.

options.label: Gains ding, costs bleed
options.consequence: Growth gets a readout; costs get only the body. Rewards feel like LitRPG and losses like grimdark.
options.sample:
[Harmonics 345. Grade A.]

The line came for the gain, cold and exact, while the fox-fire stood cold amber on her knuckles in the dark. The price came with no line at all. It came as a dry ache under the sternum that was still there at breakfast, as lips split from the heat off her own skin, as a tail that would not lie still for a day. She had to work the cost out herself.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps R48-37's law that the body pays first and still gives the reader the genre's number in the same breath, which R16-3 already asks of mechanism and system term. Inside a fight, LR11 holds the number until the finisher or the aftermath.

questions.title: How fast the numbers climb
questions.question: How often should a character's numbers move across a thread or a book?
questions.context: FOW: Band I growth 'is the fastest in a character's life', returns then diminish ('The Crystal has already solved that shape'), Stages move only by Catalyst, and a stalled practitioner builds Residual Strain. Progression fantasy (fiction where measurable growth drives the plot) pays a small reward every few chapters; cultivation novels add bottlenecks, long plateaus broken by a breakthrough.

options.label: Slow and heavy
options.consequence: Levels move a handful per arc and Stages once a book at most, with long plateaus. Each gain is rare enough to be an event.

options.label: Genre rhythm
options.consequence: A small gain every few chapters, a large one at each arc's close, a Stage breakthrough as an arc's climax.

options.label: Event-bound
options.consequence: Numbers move only for a cause the reader was shown: a FOW XP event on the page, or training named in a downtime turn.

options.label: Fast young, slow old
options.consequence: Band I characters climb visibly every arc; veterans plateau and fight for single Levels, FOW's curve made plain.

questions.rec_reason: Every gain then points at a cause the reader watched, which keeps the numbers fair and traceable (R14-3), and FOW's own curve produces B's rhythm for the young and D's plateaus for the old without a quota.

questions.title: A breakthrough on the page
questions.question: When a practitioner crosses into a new Stage, how is the crossing itself written?
questions.context: FOW raises Stage only by Catalyst (Welling's is 'first genuine contact with a Wellspring current under personal pressure'), and R9-3 gives the crossing the display register: eyes first, the body under load, one splash-panel beat (a comic's full-page image). Cultivation novels give a breakthrough a whole scene, sometimes a heavenly tribulation (heaven's lightning sent against the climber). LR14 asks how the new Stage is then confirmed.

options.label: One display beat (current)
options.consequence: R9-3 stands: the crossing is one beat inside a larger scene, eyes first, body under load, the cost after. It never gets a scene of its own.
options.sample: They had him half out of the hole when it came on him, and the men on the rope saw it first: light behind his eyes, taking the iris and then the white, so that the nearest of them let go of his collar. Every tendon in Qanik's neck stood out. Something in his chest gave, cleanly, a seam letting out under load. Then he was flat on the ice with blood running from his nose, and Welling was in him, and the rest of the morning was rope and cold.

options.label: Cultivation set piece
options.consequence: The crossing gets its own scene in stages: the plateau, the Catalyst worked through, the body remade sense by sense, the Stage named, the price. Once per character per arc.
options.sample: For nine days after the lake the current he had touched would not leave him and would not finish. It sat under his breastbone like a held note. On the tenth Qanik went out alone to the hole they had cut for him and sat on the ice beside it with his hands bare, and let it run where it wanted, which was down every fear he owned, the drowning first. By noon his sweat had frozen on him in a crust. By dusk the current under the whole lake was sounding in his teeth, and he knew its name, and his own Stage, and what both had cost.

options.label: In the crisis, line after
options.consequence: It happens inside the danger that is its Catalyst, written from the body; the line lands as the danger breaks and the Catalyst completes, never mid-exchange (LR11). R9-3's splash beat goes to the crisis.
options.sample:
Under the ice the current found him before the cold did. It came in through the soles with a direction to it, and the hum Qanik had lived with since boyhood stopped being noise and pointed up. He followed it. His hands found the edge of the hole by a pull he could not have named, and the men hauled him out blue. On the ice, with a hide-coat round him and seal fat in his mouth, the line came.

[Stage II, Welling. Apprentice.]

options.label: The world answers
options.consequence: The crossing is a Mystic-register event the place records: gauges jump, lamps dim, beasts and people react at a distance. WOTR's heavenly tribulation, with R53-17's bill at scale.
options.sample: At the hour Qanik went under, the one Guild gauge at the sealing station jumped off its mark, and the dogs on the lines went flat on their bellies and would not get up. Women came out of the hide tents and stood in the snow looking at the lake, which had done nothing anyone could see. Out on the ice the men on the rope felt it come up the rope into their hands like a fish taking. Then they were hauling, and the boy came up blue with Welling in him, and every blubber lamp in the station had burned down a finger in the time it took.

questions.rec_reason: FOW's Catalysts already happen in danger, so the crossing stays in the body where grimdark wants it, R9-3's one splash beat lands on the crisis, and the line arrives where LR7, LR11 and LR12 put it, with LR14's hall to follow.

questions.title: Confirming a new Stage
questions.question: When a practitioner crosses into a new Stage, how is the new Stage confirmed on the page?
questions.context: FOW's Catalyst for Welling is 'first genuine contact with a Wellspring current under personal pressure'. LR23 asks how the crossing itself is written; this asks how it is confirmed. System novels flash the notice at once; Solo Leveling's drama is a re-measurement that contradicts the record; cultivation sects announce a breakthrough before the whole hall.

options.label: The line in the moment
options.consequence: The readout lands as the Catalyst completes: the Crystal's line if K2 opens screens, a trained count if not. The System novel's notice.
options.sample:
Qanik came up through the hole on a pull he could not have named. He lay on the ice. The cold went into him through the hide, and the line arrived before his breath did, whole and plain.

[Stage II, Welling. Apprentice.]

Then the men had him, rolling him into a hide-coat and rubbing his feet, and somebody put seal fat in his mouth and said wet wood burns eventually. He held the line behind his breastbone all the way to the fire.

options.label: A private re-assay
options.consequence: Nobody knows for days; the body hints, and a Measurewright's coil confirms it in a kitchen or an office. The re-measure beat, quiet and personal.
options.sample: Qanik came out of the lake blue and coughing, and they put him by the fire with seal fat in his mouth and said wet wood burns eventually. Over the next week it was the cups that gave him away. He set every one down too hard. On the eighth day the Measurewright put the boy's wrist in the coil, and the needle went past the place it had stopped in the autumn. "Welling," the man said, and wrote it, and Qanik's mother sat down.

options.label: A public re-assay
options.consequence: The re-assay is a rite before witnesses, read aloud and entered on the Reckoner's roll: the sect's ranking ceremony, in WOTR's institutions.
options.sample: They held the re-assay in the Seat's hall with the doors open, because a boy who came back from under the ice was a matter for everyone. Qanik stood on the cold flags in a borrowed hide-coat. The Measurewright read the coil and spoke it to the room: "Stage II. Welling. Apprentice." The Reckoner wrote it on the roll. An old woman by the door said, "By the fire," and then the whole hall was saying it, and his mother was saying it loudest.

options.label: Unconfirmed, only shown
options.consequence: No readout: the new Stage shows in what he can now do and in what people start calling him, with the figures left to the notes. The Western way.
options.sample: Qanik came out of the lake blue and coughing, and they put him by the fire with seal fat in his mouth and said wet wood burns eventually. Nobody brought a coil. Over the winter the camp marked other things: that he set cups down too hard, that the dogs went quiet when he crossed the lines, that the old sealers had started asking him where the current ran. By the Thin Weeks the girls were calling him Underice. Nobody wrote anything down.

questions.rec_reason: The bearer's own line already lands as the Catalyst completes (LR7's B, LR23), so this asks how the world learns it. Stages move rarely, so each can afford a hall: the cultivation sect's ceremony and the LitRPG reveal at once, through the Reckoner's roll WOTR already keeps, while the crossing itself stays in the body.

questions.title: Build talk in dialogue
questions.question: Who may talk exact numbers and builds in dialogue?
questions.context: Your 2026-09-12 ruling on R14-B: stats 'can be named, but do it like how people talk about stats in LitRPGs like Unbound'. R52-05 keeps exact-number speech to 'Lambert, the Measurewrights, clerks and anyone reading an instrument'; 'everyone else rounds'. The Primer already talks builds (a build is a chosen spread of stats): specialists 'produce peaks by accepting valleys elsewhere'.

options.label: Counters only
options.consequence: Keeps R52-05: Lambert, Measurewrights, clerks and instrument readers say exact figures; everyone else talks in Grades, rounds or guesses.
options.sample: Lambert read the tape twice and set it down square to the table's edge. "Harmonics three hundred and forty-five. On a Level of a hundred and forty-five. Ardency a hundred and fifty-five. Dominion a hundred and fifty." Lorn did not look at the figures. "So she hears like a saint and couldn't hit a door." "Roughly." "Then she stays off the wall," Lorn said, "and on the stair, where she can hear them coming up it."

options.label: Ranked practitioners too
options.consequence: Any ranked practitioner talks his own and others' numbers exactly and argues builds, as in Unbound; commoners still round. R52-05 widens.
options.sample: Lambert read the tape twice and set it square to the table's edge. "Harmonics three hundred and forty-five, on a Level of a hundred and forty-five." "Two-forty-five Dexterity," Lorn said. "One-fifty-five Ardency. She's put everything into hearing and paid for it with her hands. Peaks bought with valleys." "The Primer says the valleys are where they die." "The Primer never fought on a stair," Lorn said. "Put her on the stair."

options.label: Theorycraft scenes
options.consequence: B, plus whole scenes where a party theorycrafts (plans builds and pairings from the numbers) at length, as the LitRPG serials Delve and He Who Fights With Monsters do.
options.sample: Lambert laid the tape between them and Lorn turned it with one finger. "Three-forty-five Harmonics. She hears a man's wrists before he moves them. One-fifty-five Ardency, so she can't finish what she hears. Pair her with a hitter." "Ardency at B or better," Lambert said, "and Resilience to take what she can't ward, because her Dominion is a hundred and fifty and covers nobody but herself." "Then the hitter stands where she points." "And she points first," Lambert said, writing it down. "Every time."

questions.rec_reason: It carries your Unbound ruling through: the people whose lives turn on these numbers talk them, while commoners keep their folk words and R53-18's awe. Whole planning scenes (C) earn their length only when a stake rides on them.

questions.title: Gamer slang
questions.question: Where may gamer slang appear: min-max (pile points into one stat and starve another), dump stat (the one starved), aggro (an enemy's attention), cooldown (the wait before a skill works again)?
questions.context: R48-13 (2026-09-26): 'characters may talk modern; narration keeps a timeless register', and R51-05 allows technology metaphors only 'if the POV's own culture has the thing'; no WOTR culture has a video game. LitRPG narrators use this slang freely. verify_scene's modern-word list does not include it yet. Slang in thought is asked in the interiority section.

options.label: Speech, by ear
options.consequence: Current law: gamer slang in a mouth whose voice would carry it; narration stays timeless. verify_scene adds these words to its narration watch-list.
options.sample: Do-hyun sat on the edge of the proving floor with his wrist in a basin of snowmelt. "You min-maxed," Ha-eun said, crouching beside him. "Every point in your hands and nothing in your legs. He walked round you." "He was fast." "He was one step to the left. You had no floor." The hall's old steward went past with his broom and did not look at either of them, and the straw matting he swept smelled of sweat and lamp-oil.

options.label: Narration too
options.consequence: Close-POV narration may carry gamer slang: the LitRPG narrator's voice. R48-13 and R51-05 give way for these words, and verify_scene leaves them alone.
options.sample: Do-hyun had min-maxed himself into a corner, every point in his hands and nothing in his legs, and the other boy had simply walked round him. Now he sat on the edge of the proving floor with his wrist in a basin of snowmelt and his best technique on a long cooldown. "He was fast," he said. "He was one step to the left," Ha-eun said. The hall's old steward went past with his broom, and the straw matting smelled of sweat and lamp-oil.

options.label: The world's own words
options.consequence: WOTR coins its own phrases and uses them even in speech: 'peaks bought with valleys' for min-maxing, 'on the floor' for a dump stat. The slang never appears.
options.sample: Do-hyun sat on the edge of the proving floor with his wrist in a basin of snowmelt. "You put it all in the hands," Ha-eun said, crouching beside him. "Peaks bought with valleys, and he walked through the valley. Your legs are on the floor." "He was fast." "He was one step to the left." The hall's old steward went past with his broom and did not look at either of them, and the straw matting he swept smelled of sweat and lamp-oil.

questions.rec_reason: Speech is where the genre's banter lives and R48-13 already allows it there, while narration keeps the Victorian surface that gamer slang would crack, which is the job R51-05 does.

questions.title: Item cards
questions.question: Does an item's Tier and worth ever reach the page as a set-off card?
questions.context: R46-2 names the item ladder, each Tier with a Latin form and a Grade band (Proofed, Probatum, Grade D), and proof-marks are standing texture. LitRPG gives loot a tooltip (a small panel of name, rarity, numbers and a line of lore), a habit the game Dark Souls made famous for its lore. How price, grade and provenance read in prose is DS12.

options.label: Item card, once
options.consequence: A set-off card at purchase or appraisal: Tier, Latin form, Grade band, maker, stamp, price, one line of lore. Once per item, never reprinted.
options.sample:
The gunsmith set a paper of rounds on the counter and broke one out for her to see. The brass carried the Guild's stamp under the rim, a small square with the probatum bar through it.

> PROOFED SHOT · Probatum · Grade D
> Guild-stamped at the Hallenfeld proof-house. 1 silver the round.
> Tested in a cold barrel by a man who signed for it.

Captain Sallow counted out twelve silver and did not haggle. Nobody haggled over proofed shot in a winter like this one.

options.label: In-world slip only
options.consequence: The tooltip exists only as a document read in the scene (an issue slip, an auction lot, an assay certificate) in its institution's house style (R51-33).
options.sample: The gunsmith wrote the issue slip in his fair hand while she waited: Shot, proofed. Probatum. Grade D. Hallenfeld proof-house, stamp entered. Twelve rounds at one silver the round. He blotted it, turned it to face her, and waited for her mark. Captain Sallow signed. She folded the slip into her pocket-book behind the wire from the Seat and took the paper of rounds without looking inside it, because nobody haggled over proofed shot in a winter like this one.

options.label: No card
options.consequence: Tier and worth reach the page only through prose, as DS12 decides. Nothing is set off.
options.sample: The gunsmith broke a round out of the paper and turned it under the lamp so she could read the base. The Guild's stamp sat under the rim with the probatum bar through it: Proofed, Grade D, tested at the Hallenfeld proof-house by a man who had signed for it. One silver the round. Captain Sallow counted out twelve and did not haggle. Nobody haggled over proofed shot in a winter like this one.

questions.rec_reason: The tooltip is one of the genre's real pleasures, and R46-2 has already built every field it needs from canon; once per item, at the moment of buying or appraising, keeps it an event.

questions.title: Titles and achievements
questions.question: Where do titles come from, and do they carry any mechanical weight?
questions.context: R50-21 lets an NPC coin a Third Name (the title the world gives a practitioner), and it sticks only if you keep it. Canon's rank token bears 'the holder's certified rank' and nothing else. LitRPG Systems award titles at feats, often with stat bonuses, as The Primal Hunter does; cultivation novels spread titles by rumour and sect decree.

options.label: People's names only
options.consequence: Current practice: titles are Third Names and epithets that people give and use. No notice and no effect.
options.sample: By the end of the Thin Weeks the posting houses were calling him Snowpost, and the name reached Hallenfeld before he did. Nobody entered it anywhere. The quartermaster used it to his face. The girls in the Seat's kitchen used it behind his back. The boy himself, who was fifteen and had lost two toes to the road, never once said it aloud. He signed the courier book with his mark, as he always had.

options.label: Guild commendations
options.consequence: The Guild may also enter a commendation on a registration and strike its mark on the token: legal and social weight, no stat effect. Third Names carry on as now.
options.sample: The commendation came down the corridor in the spring post: Entered for service, the Thin Weeks, the Seat road. The proof-house at Hallenfeld struck a small mark on the back of his token beside the rank. It bought him nothing at a counter. At every posting house on the road, though, the keeper turned the token over, read the mark, and gave him the bed nearest the stove, and he was fifteen and slept there like the dead.

options.label: Continuum titles
options.consequence: The Continuum grants a title at a feat, with a stated effect on the sheet, as LitRPG Systems do. New canon, and it needs K2's D with LR22's B.
options.sample:
On the last night of the Thin Weeks, alone at a posting house with the fire nearly out, the boy felt a line arrive behind his breastbone.

[Title: Snowpost. Endurance on the road; the cold counts lighter.]

He lay awake a long time after it, trying to feel his toes, the eight he still had, and could not tell whether they were any warmer than they had been the night before.

questions.rec_reason: It gives the genre's achievement a real object inside WOTR's own institutions and keeps power in the Crystal, where FOW puts it, while Third Names keep working as they do.

questions.title: Quests and contracts
questions.question: Does WOTR have quests, and in what in-world form?
questions.context: Canon already has 'contracted bounty work' and the Guild's 'register of who cleared the gallery' on the Well roads. Solo Leveling issues quests with an objective, a reward and a penalty; xianxia sects (orders in Chinese immortal-cultivation fiction) post tasks for contribution points; Western grimdark has jobs and debts. The table's Fronts and Scene Menu already throw up hooks.

options.label: Contract boards
options.consequence: Guild and Crown contracts posted with terms, pay and the clearance register: the quest board as a Draw Age notice. Hooks gain a stated reward and penalty.

options.label: Named commissions
options.consequence: Sealed Guild commissions to a named practitioner, with objective, fee and penalty for failure: Solo Leveling's quest window as a letter.

options.label: Continuum tasks
options.consequence: The Continuum itself sets tasks with stated rewards. New canon, and it makes the world's cosmology a quest-giver.

options.label: No quests
options.consequence: Work arrives as people asking, Fronts moving and debts coming due, as now.

questions.rec_reason: Bounty contracts and a clearance register are already canon, so a board costs no new cosmology, and posted terms give the LitRPG reader a reward and a penalty to reckon with.

questions.title: Sheets at chapter and arc ends
questions.question: Do chapters or arcs end with a character sheet?
questions.context: WOTR's figures live in the author notes as a Stat Ledger (R14-6-CHECK29), below the Notes heading the checker never reads (R54-12). Progression fantasy often closes a chapter or volume with the hero's updated sheet, set outside the scene for the reader; Western novels keep appendices for a book's end, as Tolkien did. R20C-32 warns that cards drift.

options.label: Full sheet at arc end
options.consequence: Each arc closes with the POV's full sheet from the card, in the Guild's tape style. Book mode only.

options.label: Changes at chapter end
options.consequence: Each chapter closes with a short block of what moved and why, above the notes; roleplay turns keep it in the notes.

options.label: Both
options.consequence: Changes per chapter and the full sheet at each arc's end. The most LitRPG, and the most figures to source.

options.label: None in the text
options.consequence: Sheets stay on the wiki cards and in the notes; the text carries only what scenes show.

questions.rec_reason: A short changes block shows the climb at the genre's steady rate and sources only what moved; a full sheet freezes figures the cards are still revising.

questions.title: A number not yet in canon
questions.question: What does a readout do when the figure it should show is not in canon?
questions.context: R12-5: 'Never invent a number. Unchanged and absolute... Unspecified means flagged as estimate.' A mouth can hedge ('call it four hundred'); a printed readout cannot. Yoko's card gives her reserve as about 185,000 EU, marked estimate with no exact source. In So I'm a Spider, So What?, a Japanese light novel, appraisal lines fill in as the skill grows.

options.label: Blank the field
options.consequence: The instrument prints what canon has and marks the rest beyond reading, like an appraisal still growing. Gaps become texture, and the notes log them.
options.sample:
The coil's tape ran out its lines and stopped short on the last.

> Harmonics 345 A · past the instability line
> η 0.60
> Reserve: BEYOND READING

The Measurewright tapped the last line with his pencil. "Field coil," he said. "The big one at Hallenfeld would reach it. This one runs out of winding." Yoko had not asked. She folded the tape into her glove anyway, last line inward.

options.label: Print the estimate, marked
options.consequence: The readout prints the figure with the instrument's own hedge (a range, 'uncertain past the third place'), and the notes log it as estimate.
options.sample:
The coil's tape ran out its lines.

> Harmonics 345 A · past the instability line
> η 0.60
> Reserve ~185,000 EU · uncertain past the third place

The Measurewright tapped the last line with his pencil. "That one's a guess with a stamp on it," he said. "Any coil this size would tell you the same lie and swear to it." Yoko folded the tape into her glove, last line inward, and carried it back out into the cold yard, where the split halves were knocking onto the woodpile one after another for the Thin Weeks.

options.label: Drop the line
options.consequence: A readout prints only sourced fields; estimates stay in the notes, and the box is shorter.
options.sample:
The coil's tape ran out two lines and stopped.

> Harmonics 345 A · past the instability line
> η 0.60

The Measurewright tore it off and handed it across. He said nothing about her reserve. Yoko, who could smell what a man left out of a sentence, did not ask him to. She folded the tape into her glove and went back out into the cold yard, where the woodpile was going up against the wall.

options.label: Derive, then print
options.consequence: The figure is worked out from FOW's tables (the Essence Ledger bands for the Stage) before posting, printed plain, and logged in the notes as derived. R12-5's on-page flag gives way.
options.sample:
The coil's tape ran out its lines.

> Harmonics 345 A · past the instability line
> η 0.60
> Reserve 185,000 EU

The Measurewright read all three aloud in the same flat voice, the reserve no differently from the rest, and initialled the tape at the foot. Yoko folded it into her glove, last line inward, and went back out into the cold yard.

questions.rec_reason: An instrument with an error bar is honest period texture: it keeps R12-5's flag on the page where the reader can see it, and the hedge feeds the world's well-earned distrust of readings.

sections.title: Combat on the page
sections.intro: How a fight reads blow by blow, and what surrounds it. Numbers inside a fight belong to LR; named attacks, mid-fight explanation and the watching crowd to MY. These settle the choreography, the ceremony and what a fight leaves behind.

questions.title: Which martial vocabulary names the moves
questions.question: Which martial vocabulary traces a duel on the page?
questions.context: This reopens R48-33, ruled 2026-09-26: 'the move by its fencing name', in HEMA (Historical European Martial Arts: Vom Tag, the high guard; Zornhau, the wrath-cut; Indes, in the same instant), per R13-6-HEMA_VOCAB. Japanese fencing has its own words: jōdan, high guard; ma-ai, fighting distance; kiri-otoshi, cutting down through his cut; sen no sen, striking as he commits.

options.label: HEMA for everyone
options.consequence: R48-33 and R13-6-HEMA_VOCAB stand: German and English fencing names trace every duel, a Shirogane or lineage-hall fighter's included. verify keeps its one word list.
options.sample: The Greymane rider opened from Vom Tag and threw a Zornhau at the crown, heavy in the shoulder from years of cutting down off a saddle. The Shirogane duellist went up into the same guard and cut Indes on the rider's own line. The blades met in the bind. His rode over. It opened the left forearm to the bone a hand above the wrist, and the rider's grip failed. From the rail the armsmaster had counted the measure at two paces, and the Shirogane man had stolen half of it before the Zornhau left the shoulder.

options.label: By the fighter's school
options.consequence: Each fighter's moves carry his own school's names whoever watches: Japanese for the Shirogane, HEMA for Greymane, hall forms for the lineage halls. verify --combat takes a word list per school.
options.sample: The Greymane rider opened from Vom Tag and threw a Zornhau at the crown, heavy in the shoulder from years of cutting down off a saddle. The Shirogane duellist rose into jōdan and gave him kiri-otoshi, sen no sen, as the cut committed. The blades met. His rode over. It opened the left forearm to the bone a hand above the wrist, and the rider's grip failed. From the rail the armsmaster had counted the ma-ai at two paces, and the Shirogane man had stolen half of it before the Zornhau left the shoulder.

options.label: By the POV's own school
options.consequence: Narration names every move in the POV's own training (a Moto POV calls a diagonal cut kesa-giri, a Greymane POV a Zornhau); a foreign school's word arrives in a mouth. verify takes per-school lists.
options.sample: The Greymane rider came up into a horseman's jōdan, elbows wide, and threw kesa-giri at the neck, heavy in the shoulder from years of cutting down off a saddle. The Shirogane duellist rose into jōdan with him and gave him kiri-otoshi. The blades met. His rode over. It opened the left forearm to the bone a hand above the wrist, and the rider's grip failed. On the far rail the Greymane men were still roaring Zornhau at a cut that had already lost. The Shirogane armsmaster had counted the ma-ai at two paces.

options.label: Plain English mechanics
options.consequence: School names leave the page; moves are traced in plain words for height, line, distance and timing. R48-33's 'fencing name' clause is struck and the HEMA warning retired.
options.sample: The Greymane rider lifted his sword high and threw a cut at the crown, heavy in the shoulder from years of cutting down off a saddle. The Shirogane duellist lifted his own and cut straight down onto the rider's line as it came. The blades met. His rode over. It opened the left forearm to the bone a hand above the wrist, and the rider's grip failed. From the rail the armsmaster had judged the distance at two paces, and the Shirogane man had stolen half of it before the rider's cut left the shoulder.

questions.rec_reason: It puts Japanese, Chinese and Korean fencing words on the page whenever an Eastern-trained POV fights or watches, keeps HEMA for Western POVs, and keeps WOTR's POV discipline: no narration knows a school its viewpoint never trained in.

questions.title: Declaring name and line before a duel
questions.question: Do fighters declare their name and lineage before a duel, and how much of it reaches the page?
questions.context: Nanori is the Japanese war-tale custom of calling out name, father, grandfather and deeds before single combat; wuxia (Chinese martial-hero fiction) has the challenger name himself, and Homer's Glaucus recites his line to Diomedes. No rule covers it. R48-43 allows 'one crafted, eloquent speech at a big moment', and R60-01-BRUTAL_LETHALITY ends most fights 'in the first seconds'.

options.label: Fights open cold
options.consequence: No rule is written. Fights open without declarations; a fighter's line surfaces later, in talk or in a document.
options.sample: The Greymane rider walked his horse into the ford until the water came to its knees, and stopped there, and drew. Across the water the Shirogane duellist stepped off the bank onto the ice shelf with his sandals in his hand and set them down behind him in a neat pair. Neither man spoke. The horse blew; its breath stood white between them and thinned. The Shirogane man came forward through it at a walk, and the rider put his heels in.

options.label: Name and house, one line
options.consequence: A new rule allows a one-sentence declaration (name, house, at most one deed) before a duel in any culture; longer recitals are cut.
options.sample: The Greymane rider walked his horse into the ford until the water came to its knees. "Aldric Osgarson, who rides for Greymane," he called, and drew. Across the water the Shirogane duellist stepped onto the ice shelf and set his sandals down behind him in a neat pair. "Shirogane," he said. He gave the house and kept the rest. The horse blew; its breath stood white between them. The Shirogane man came forward through it at a walk, and the rider put his heels in.

options.label: Full declaration, free
options.consequence: Full declarations become legal wherever the culture keeps the custom (Japonic, Korean, Chinese, Norse-register), outside R48-43's one-speech count. A refused answer, or a nameless opponent, is written as a beat.
options.sample: The Greymane rider walked his horse into the ford until the water came to its knees. "I am Aldric, son of Osgar, son of Wulfstan, who rode under the grey banner before the Banner Houses broke. I have held the Hallenfeld road since my nineteenth winter. Send me a man worth the cold." Across the water the Shirogane duellist set his sandals down on the ice shelf in a neat pair. "Kaname of the Shirogane, second son of Hideaki, third of our line to hold the assay at the Seat. I have cut better riders on worse ice. Get off the horse."

options.label: Full declaration, with a price
options.consequence: Full declarations are legal but count as the scene's crafted speech under R48-43, and the world does not wait: an opponent may close measure, or shoot, while the recital runs.
options.sample: The Greymane rider walked his horse into the ford until the water came to its knees. "I am Aldric, son of Osgar, son of Wulfstan, who rode under the grey banner before the Banner Houses broke. I have held the Hallenfeld road since my nineteenth winter..." The Shirogane duellist had left his sandals on the bank while the rider was still on his grandfather. By the Hallenfeld road he was on the ice shelf. He was inside the horse's reach before anyone was asked to be worth the cold. "Your line is long," Kaname said. "Mine is shorter."

questions.rec_reason: It gives the war-tale and saga ceremony its full voice and keeps R60-01's lethality: the recital costs time, and an enemy who spends that time well is the grimdark answer to it.

questions.title: Stillness, traced passes, or the long fight
questions.question: What shape does a duel take on the page: stillness and one decisive cut, several traced passes, or a long escalating fight?
questions.context: This reopens R48-33, ruled 2026-09-26 ('every exchange traced'). R60-01-BRUTAL_LETHALITY ends most fights 'in the first seconds', and Verdict Grammar says 'the tension lives in the read' (R1-1-VERDICT_GRAMMAR). Chanbara (Japanese sword films) hold stillness, then one draw; shōnen manga (action comics for boys) stretch one fight across chapters, a tell under R5-B-MANHWA_DIRECTIVE_REPEALED. SP2 sets scene tempo; this sets duel shape.

options.label: Traced passes, as now
options.consequence: R48-33 and R13-4-COMBAT_FLOOR stand: every duel runs traced passes, each meaningful exchange carrying the floor, at the length R13-4-DENSITY_BUDGET sets. Nothing escalates for its own sake.
options.sample: Aldric opened from the high guard with a cut to the head, and Kaname took it near his own hilt, bound, and wound his point in toward the throat. Aldric stepped off the line. Second pass. Aldric feinted low, came over the top, and caught the Shirogane man's left shoulder through the quilted coat, a shallow cut that bled into the cloth. Kaname changed his grip. On the third pass Aldric was a hair late, and the cut opened the inside of his thigh high, over the femoral.

options.label: Stillness, then one cut
options.consequence: Duels between trained fighters default to a long read and a one-sentence strike; R13-4's floor is packed into the read before and the aftermath after. Multi-pass duels become the exception.
options.sample: They stood in the yard for as long as a broth takes to go cold. Snow settled on Aldric's shoulders and stayed. Kaname held his sword low and to the right, and his weight sat in neither foot that anyone on the rail could find. Aldric's breath went out white, came back, went out. On the fourth breath his front heel lifted to take the step. Kaname was already through. The cut opened the inside of Aldric's thigh high, over the femoral, and the blood reached the snow before Aldric knew to look down.

options.label: Long escalating duels
options.consequence: Practitioners may duel at length, trading named forms and deeper reveals across a scene or chapter. R5-B's escalation tell is struck for duels; R60-03-HARD_RESERVE_CLOCK is what ends them.
options.sample: By the twentieth pass both men steamed in the cold. Aldric had a scalp cut running blood into his left eye; Kaname had stopped using his left hand. Twice the Shirogane man had shown a form of his house and twice Aldric had answered it, and the betting on the rail had stopped. Aldric's reserve was near the bottom. The Pressure off him had thinned to a draught. Then Kaname showed the third form, low, rising inside the bind, and the cut opened the inside of Aldric's thigh over the femoral.

options.label: Shape follows the grammar
options.consequence: A rule ties duel shape to the four combat grammars: Verdict still then one cut, Blade traced passes, Percussion and Expenditure by attrition; practitioners escalate while reserve lasts. R60-01 holds for the unranked.
options.sample: Aldric fenced. He opened from the high guard, bound, wound, came round again, and each pass cost him breath in the cold. Kaname answered none of it with a pass of his own. He gave ground, took a shallow cut across the shoulder through the quilting, and kept his attention on Aldric's front heel. On the fifth pass the heel lifted early. Kaname went through on that beat, once, and the cut opened the inside of the thigh over the femoral. Aldric sat down in the snow with both hands on the wound.

questions.rec_reason: WOTR already has four combat grammars; letting shape follow them gives chanbara stillness to Verdict fighters, HEMA passes to Blade fighters and the long shōnen fight to practitioners whose reserve can pay for it, while ordinary men still die fast.

questions.title: Memory inside a fight
questions.question: May a fight stop for a memory, and whose?
questions.context: R49-06 lets memories run 'a page or more when they matter' but does not place them; a combat turn is six seconds (R47-11-TIME_AND_ENERGY), and written scenes keep the POV lock (R48-40). Shōnen manga freeze a fight for a page of the fighter's past, or the dying opponent's; Western grimdark stays in the present and lets the past arrive in the aftermath.

options.label: Memory after, never during
options.consequence: Inside a fight, memory is held to a clause; flashbacks sit before or after it. R49-06 gains that limit.
options.sample: The blade went low and came up inside the bind, and Aldric knew the form before it finished. He turned his hips. The cut took him across the ribs instead of the belly and grated on bone. He gave a pace, and another, and kept his point on the Shirogane man's eyes while the blood ran warm into his belt and down the inside of his leg. Whoever had taught him that turn could wait for the cot and the lamp. Here there was the next pass.

options.label: A few lines of memory
options.consequence: A memory of a few lines may open inside a held instant, tied to the move on the page (where it was learned, who taught it); the fight resumes at once.
options.sample: The blade went low and came up inside the bind, and Aldric knew the form before it finished. His uncle Edmund in the long barn at home, a hay-fork for a sword, laughing as the tines came up under the boy's guard for the ninth time. The low ones always come back up. He turned his hips. The cut took him across the ribs instead of the belly and grated on bone. He gave a pace and kept his point on the Shirogane man's eyes while the blood ran warm into his belt.

options.label: Full flashback, POV only
options.consequence: The POV may take a full flashback, a page or more, frozen inside one turning exchange, once per fight. The POV lock holds; the opponent's past reaches the page only through what the POV knows.
options.sample: The blade went low and came up inside the bind. Aldric was ten, in the long barn at home, and the barn smelled of wet hay and of the dog that slept in the oat bin. Uncle Edmund held a hay-fork for a sword. He was laughing. Nine times the tines came up under the boy's guard. Nine times Edmund put him on his back in the chaff, and the ninth time he left him there and said, The low ones always come back up. Then Aldric was in the yard again with the blade already in him, turning his hips too late to save the ribs.

options.label: The opponent's past too
options.consequence: C, plus the opponent's past as a marked italic passage, usually as he strikes or falls. R48-40's POV lock breaks for that passage only.
options.sample:
The blade went low and came up inside the bind, and the cut grated on Aldric's ribs. Kaname drew back to finish it.

*Twenty winters gone, in the Shirogane hall at the Seat, a boy knelt on boards cold enough to take the skin off his knees. He held a practice sword over his head until his arms shook. His father was watching. His elder brother had held it longer. Second son, the house said every morning, with its seating and its rice.*

In the yard Kaname brought the blade down, and Aldric's met it a finger's width from his collarbone.

questions.rec_reason: It takes the shōnen reframe at full length, which R49-06 already licenses, and keeps the POV lock, so the opponent stays someone the reader has to read from outside.

questions.title: The rival bond
questions.question: Does WOTR run the recurring rival, the opponent who comes back fight after fight with respect on both sides?
questions.context: Shōnen manga build a series on the rival who returns; Chinese martial fiction has the honoured enemy and the sworn brother; Japanese war tales mourn the enemy they kill. WOTR leans the other way: 'Death can happen, if earned' (R48-31-STAKES), most fights end in seconds (R60-01), and a battle moves one relationship by a 'single unrepeatable act' (R2-5-SINGLE_ACT_RULE).

options.label: No standing rivals
options.consequence: No rule is written. Enemies who live are rare and unplanned; respect for an opponent shows once, in the aftermath, and death stays on the table every fight.

options.label: Rivals who chose to spare
options.consequence: A rival may recur, but each survival is a choice someone made and paid for on the Ledger: a debt, a scar, a witness to the mercy. R48-31 stands.

options.label: Rival as a thread's spine
options.consequence: Each POV thread may carry a named rival whose fights run across arcs as a relationship, with rematches tracked as a Front. Death stays possible, though the thread pulls against it.

options.label: Rival pairs among NPCs
options.consequence: Rival pairs run between NPCs as world texture (two duellists the Seat bets on), never aimed at Isaac's characters unless his play makes one.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the Eastern rival bond and makes every rematch cost something on the Ledger, which is the grimdark price of the trope.

questions.title: What joins the wound when a fight ends
questions.question: What joins the clinical wound and the aftermath when someone dies by the blade?
questions.context: R48-34's 'full clinical gore' and R48-38's aftermath beat stay in every option. Japanese sword drama adds rites around a kill (chiburi, the flick that throws blood off the blade; resheathing; courtesies owed the dead), and the war tales give the fallen grief and beauty (mono no aware, the sadness of passing things). R5-C2 ties elegy to 'a named concrete thing'.

options.label: Clinical, as now
options.consequence: R48-34 and R48-38 stand alone: wounds by anatomy and blood loss, the stink, the dressing. No ceremony or elegiac image is asked for after a kill.
options.sample: Aldric sat down in the snow with both hands clamped on his thigh, and the femoral put blood through his fingers in pulses until the pulses slowed. His lips went grey. He tried to say something about his horse and lost the end of it. The yard stank. Hot iron, and his bowels, which had let go. Kaname stood three paces off with his own sleeve red from the shoulder cut, breathing hard, and waited for it to finish.

options.label: Add the killing rites
options.consequence: A rule adds the rites of the kill where the killer's culture keeps them (the blood-flick, resheathing, courtesies to the dead, a name asked and kept), on top of the clinical floor.
options.sample: Aldric sat down in the snow with both hands clamped on his thigh, and the femoral put blood through his fingers in pulses until the pulses slowed. His lips went grey. The yard stank of hot iron and of his bowels, which had let go. Kaname flicked the blade once, hard. A line of red dots crossed the snow. He wiped the rest on folded paper and slid the steel home. Then he knelt at the edge of the blood. "Your grandfather's name," he said. "Once more. I will carry it."

options.label: Add the elegiac image
options.consequence: A rule adds one elegiac image after a death, tied to a concrete thing (R5-C2-ELEGY_CONCRETE_THING), on top of the clinical floor. The rot and the stink stay in.
options.sample: Aldric sat down in the snow with both hands clamped on his thigh, and the femoral put blood through his fingers in pulses until the pulses slowed. He tried to say something about his horse and lost the end of it. The yard stank of hot iron and opened bowels. When it was over the blood lay round him dark at the middle and pink at its edge. Frost stood on his eyelashes. Over the Seat the aurora had come up green, and on the line his grey horse went on blowing at the cold.

options.label: Rites and image, by culture
options.consequence: Both, keyed to culture: Japonic, Korean and Chinese killers carry the rites; the elegiac image belongs to any POV whose culture mourns that way. The clinical floor holds everywhere.
options.sample: Aldric sat down in the snow with both hands clamped on his thigh, and the femoral put blood through his fingers until the pulses slowed. He tried to say something about his horse and lost the end of it. The yard stank of hot iron and of his bowels, which had let go. Kaname flicked the blade once. A line of red dots crossed the snow. He wiped the steel on folded paper, slid it home, and laid the paper on the dead man's chest. Frost stood on Aldric's eyelashes. On the line the grey horse went on blowing at the cold.

questions.rec_reason: It adds the two things the Eastern sword tradition does best around a killing, ceremony and grief, without letting either wash the blood off.

questions.title: How a battle is told
questions.question: Where does a battle with formations live on the page: in the ranks, on the commander's hill, or both?
questions.context: The Mass Combat Craft Guide runs three registers (Close, one man in the press; Line, the unit's cohesion; Field, the whole engagement, 'used sparingly') and R1-3-NAME_THREE_RULE allows three heads. Romance of the Three Kingdoms and the manga Kingdom tell war as order of battle and stratagem; Abercrombie's The Heroes tells it from the ditch. VO2 decides roving narration; this decides where the battle is told.

options.label: Soldier's eye, as now
options.consequence: R1-3 and the Mass Combat Guide stand: battles run mostly in the Close and Line registers and the Field is rationed. A stratagem is felt in the ranks as confusion.
options.sample: All Genta had of the battle was the back of the man in front of him and a strip of grey sky. The riders hit somewhere off to the left, a noise like a cart going over a bridge, and the whole block shoved sideways and his straw boots slid on the ice. Somebody's pike came down across his helmet. Blood ran into his collar, his own or not. The file-leader shouted a word he could not hear, then another, and the ranks in front came back onto him all at once. Genta went down under their weight with the ice ringing against his ear.

options.label: Stratagem from the hill
options.consequence: Battles open in the Field register from a commander's POV as an order of battle (banners, houses, blocks), and the stratagem is told as it unfolds. The guide's Field ration lifts for a battle built on a ruse.
options.sample: From the ridge Hideaki had the whole of it. The Seat's foot stood at the ford in three blocks under white banners, pikes upright on the ice like a winter reed-bed. The clan riders held the far bank in two wings. He had sent the left block forward with its colours furled, and they took it for the reserve, as he had meant them to, and charged. At forty paces the banners opened and the block knelt. The ice gave. Sawn in the night and packed over with snow, it took the first rank of horses down whole.

options.label: Hill and ditch, cut
options.consequence: A battle cuts between the commander's hill and one man in the press at marked breaks, each section POV-locked; the breaks stand in for the guide's rule to 'pass through Line'. R1-3's three heads cover both.
options.sample:
On the ridge Hideaki let the clan wings shake out below him. "Now the left," he said, and the left block went forward with its colours furled.

* * *

At the ford all Genta had of the battle was the back of the man in front and a strip of grey sky. The ice under his straw boots had been sawn in the night and packed over with snow. He stood where he was put and tried to weigh nothing.

* * *

The riders took the furled block for a reserve. At forty paces the banners opened. Genta knelt with the rest, and the ice went.

options.label: Council plan, ditch battle
options.consequence: The stratagem is laid out in full at the council before the battle (the map, the cups, the officers); the battle itself stays in the ditch, where the plan meets the ice.
options.sample:
In the tent the night before, Hideaki had laid it out with three cups on the map: the left block forward with its colours furled, the ice sawn and packed over, the riders drawn onto it. Every officer there had nodded.

At the ford all Genta had of the battle was the back of the man in front and a strip of grey sky. The horses hit somewhere to the left. The block shoved sideways. Someone was shouting kneel, kneel, and the ice under Genta's own knees, which nobody had sawn, cracked anyway.

questions.rec_reason: It puts the Three Kingdoms hill and Abercrombie's ditch in the same chapter, and the marked breaks keep every section's POV clean.

sections.title: Dialogue and speech
sections.intro: How people talk, and how Eastern speech sounds once it is English. The Japonic honorific rule (R51-21) is already law; idiom banks and sayings in narration are DT7's, verse on the page DT6's, and honorifics in narration NE2's. These settle the rest.

questions.title: Speech levels and address for the Korean and Chinese strata
questions.question: How do Korean and Chinese speakers mark rank and relationship in speech?
questions.context: R51-21 gives Japonic houses 'Japanese honorifics and address forms in speech'; R20-5-FORMAL_ADDRESS has address follow the addressing culture but sets no English form for the other strata. Korean marks relationship in verb endings (speech levels, down to banmal, the bare speech of intimates and juniors) and titles like sunbae (senior); Chinese martial speech uses shifu (master) and shixiong (senior brother).

options.label: English titles only
options.consequence: R51-21 stays the only honorific rule. Korean and Chinese speakers use English titles (Master, Elder, Teacher); rank shows in who speaks first and who stands.
options.sample: Before the bout Elder Seo had called him "boy" twice and his name once, and only to correct his stance. Now she came down off the dais on her stick and stood where his blood was drying on the boards. "Master Yun," she said. Nobody in the hall moved. His second stopped unwinding the wraps from his hands. The elder studied the cut over his eye and the hand he was holding wrong. "Master Yun will want that stitched before the swelling sets."

options.label: Native address words
options.consequence: R51-21 extends: Korean speakers use their own address words (-ssi, polite; -nim, honoured; sunbae), Chinese theirs (shifu, shixiong, qianbei, an elder of another school), romanised and never italic.
options.sample: Before the bout Elder Seo had called him "ya, Tae-sik-a" and only to correct his stance. Now she came down off the dais on her stick and stood where his blood was drying on the boards. "Yun Tae-sik-ssi," she said. Nobody in the hall moved. His second, who had been unwinding the wraps from his hands, stopped. Down the bench a sunbae from the old school said it back under his breath, ssi, as if he had dropped something. The elder studied the cut over his eye. "Have that stitched, Tae-sik-ssi, before the swelling sets."

options.label: Levels carried in English
options.consequence: No foreign address words beyond the Japonic houses; speech levels live in English grammar (bare orders against full courteous forms), and a shift of level is written as an event the room hears.
options.sample: Before the bout Elder Seo had spoken to him in the short bare forms a house keeps for its children, the verbs left off her orders. "Feet. Wider. Again." Now she came down off the dais on her stick and stood where his blood was drying on the boards, and gave him the whole sentence. "Yun Tae-sik will have this cut stitched before the swelling sets, if it would please him." Nobody in the hall moved. His second stopped unwinding the wraps from his hands. The elder had added the ending that asks, and every man on the bench had heard it.

options.label: Native words and level shifts
options.consequence: Native address words as in B, and level shifts written as events as in C. R23-10-CHINESE_PHONOTACTICS still bars stacked honorifics inside names.
options.sample: Before the bout Elder Seo had called him "ya" and left the verbs off her orders. "Feet. Wider. Again." Now she came down off the dais on her stick and stood where his blood was drying on the boards. "Yun Tae-sik-ssi," she said, and then, in the full form with the ending that asks, "would you have this cut stitched before the swelling sets?" Nobody in the hall moved. His second stopped unwinding the wraps from his hands. Down the bench a sunbae from the old school sat with his mouth a little open.

questions.rec_reason: It gives the Korean and Chinese strata what the Moto already have, and makes a change of address a dramatic event, which is the strongest thing these speech systems offer fiction.

questions.title: How Eastern-register speech sounds in English
questions.question: Do Chinese and Korean speakers talk in natural English or with the flavour of a literal translation?
questions.context: Voices differ by mind and sound (R52-02-VOICE_LEVER); the Racial Voice guide is only 'a menu' (R15-1-RACIAL_VOICE_MENU); the one translated grammar in law is Aurelian's dropped copula (R52-20-AURELIAN). Translated Chinese and Korean web fiction keeps a literal flavour: humble self-reference ('this one', 'this old man'), stock threats ('you court death'), idioms rendered word for word, face named aloud.

options.label: Natural English
options.consequence: No change: Eastern-register characters speak natural English, told apart by what they notice, want and refuse (R52-02); no translated self-reference or stock formulas.
options.sample: "You've had forty years to show anyone that sword," the young man said. "I'm asking for one afternoon." Master Lu went on sweeping the step. "I showed it to a guest once," he said. "Younger than you. Better mannered. He asked the same thing, and we buried him behind the salt store." He leaned the broom on the gatepost. "Go home. Tell your hall I'm old and slow, and keep your afternoon."

options.label: Self-reference as voice slot
options.consequence: Translated self-reference becomes a slot on the R52-03 voice block ('this one', 'this old man', 'this seat'), chosen per character; the rest of the speech stays natural English.
options.sample: "This one has walked nine days to ask for one afternoon," the young man said. Master Lu swept. "This old man showed that sword to a guest once, younger than you and better mannered, who asked the same thing," he said. "We buried him behind the salt store." He leaned the broom on the gatepost. "Go home. Tell your hall the old man is slow, and keep your afternoon."

options.label: Full translated flavour
options.consequence: Literal-translation flavour becomes the register for Chinese and Korean speakers: humble and arrogant self-reference, stock threats, idioms word for word, face named in speech. The Racial Voice menu becomes law for them.
options.sample: "Old thing, you dare hide behind a broom? This junior has walked nine days to beg one move of your sword." Master Lu went on sweeping the step. "Little friend, you are courting death," he said. "This old man showed that sword to a guest once. His eyes also sat on top of his head. The grass behind the salt store has grown over him three times." He leaned the broom on the gatepost. "Go home. Your master's face is already lost. Do not throw your own after it."

options.label: Translated forms for ceremony
options.consequence: Natural English in daily talk; the translated forms (self-reference, set formulas, idioms word for word) come out at ceremony, challenge, oath, court and insult, where the shift into them is itself a beat.
options.sample: "You've had forty years to show anyone that sword," the young man said. "I'm asking for one afternoon." Master Lu went on sweeping the step. "Go home," he said. "It's cold and you're young." The young man went down on both knees on the frozen step and set his forehead to the stone. "This junior begs instruction," he said, in the old form, the one no hall may refuse at its own gate. Master Lu stopped sweeping. "Then this old man must give it," he said, and leaned the broom on the gatepost.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps everyday talk sharp and natural, which the voice law rests on, and spends the strange formal translated forms where they carry weight: challenge, oath, court and insult.

questions.title: Proverbs in speech
questions.question: How heavily do fixed sayings carry speech, and whose mouths are they in?
questions.context: R52-30 (ruled 2026-09-26) gives every NPC 'one fixed saying from the Standing Inventory'. Korean, Japanese and Chinese elders argue in proverbs, a saying answered by a saying; Sancho Panza strings them by the dozen, and saga men end a quarrel on one. DT7 decides idiom banks and sayings in narration; this sets their weight in mouths.

options.label: One saying each, as now
options.consequence: R52-30 stands: one fixed saying per NPC, from the Inventory, used where it fits.
options.sample: "He came in the Thin Weeks with nothing on his back," the old drover said. "A man like that eats out of every pot in the camp." The widow went on stacking split rounds, pale ends out. "The first bowl goes to the one who cannot fill it themselves," she said. The drover spat into the snow. He had no answer. She set another round on the stack, and after a while he went to fetch the stranger in.

options.label: Proverb duels
options.consequence: NPCs carry several fixed sayings and may argue in them at bargain, quarrel and council, a saying answered by a saying. R52-30's 'one' becomes 'several'.
options.sample: "He came in the Thin Weeks with nothing on his back," the old drover said. "Don't saddle a horse you cannot feed." He spat in the snow. The widow kept stacking. She set each round pale end out. "The first bowl goes to the one who cannot fill it themselves." "Wet wood burns eventually," he said. "A liar never dries." "Then let him dry at my fire, and we'll learn which he is." The drover chewed on that. "The dead can wait," he said at last, sour. "The cold cannot." He went to fetch the stranger in.

options.label: Duels, by age and standing
options.consequence: B, keyed to standing: elders, headmen and court speakers argue in sayings; the young speak plain, and a youth who quotes above his years is put down for it.
options.sample: "He came in the Thin Weeks with nothing on his back," the old drover said. "Don't saddle a horse you cannot feed." The widow kept stacking. "The first bowl goes to the one who cannot fill it themselves." "Wet wood burns eventually," the drover's boy put in, pleased with himself. "A liar never dries." The widow did not look up. "When you've a stack of your own, you may quote it at me." The boy went red to the ears. The drover chewed on that, sour, and went to fetch the stranger in.

questions.rec_reason: It is how sayings live in Korean, Japanese and Chinese households and in the sagas: they belong to elders, so a proverb in a young mouth is itself a beat, and the Inventories' fixed wording gets real work.

questions.title: Verse exchanged in talk
questions.question: May people answer one another in verse: a poem met with a poem, an insult met with an insult stanza?
questions.context: DT6 decides whether verse reaches the page; this asks whether it is ever traded as talk. No rule covers it, and verify reads quoted lines as prose. Heian courtiers (Japan's classical court) answered a waka (a 31-syllable poem) with a waka; Chinese banquets cap couplets, matching a line with a line; Norse and Scots poets fought in flyting (a duel of insult verses).

options.label: Verse recited, never traded
options.consequence: Verse may be sung or recited where DT6 allows, but nobody answers a poem with a poem; talk stays prose.
options.sample: The Shirogane envoy bowed at the edge of the opened ground and said his house grieved with her. The widow kept her face toward the hole. "Your house was at the ford when he died," she said. "It may grieve from there." The envoy straightened slowly. Behind her the reader went on through the winter's dead in the order they had died, and the frozen clods knocked down onto the lid, one after another, while the envoy's servants waited for him in the snow.

options.label: Courtly cultures trade verse
options.consequence: The Moto court, Eresse, the Mahuo houses and the lineage halls may offer and answer verse at rites and in court; a weak answer, or a plain one, costs face.
options.sample:
The Shirogane envoy bowed at the edge of the opened ground and gave his condolence in verse, as his house gives it:

*The far bank lost a pine to the ice.
The near bank weeps for its shadow.*

The widow kept her face toward the hole. "Your house was at the ford when he died," she said. "It may weep from there." She had answered a poem in plain words, and two of his servants looked at the snow. The envoy straightened slowly. The frozen clods knocked down onto the lid.

options.label: Each culture its own contest
options.consequence: B, plus the north's own form: Northern English and Norse-register speakers may answer in alliterative insult verse (flyting). Each culture's verse form is entered in its Inventory.
options.sample:
The Shirogane envoy bowed at the edge of the opened ground and gave his condolence in verse, as his house gives it:

*The far bank lost a pine to the ice.
The near bank weeps for its shadow.*

The widow kept her face toward the hole and answered in the north's own measure, without a pause:

*Mint-men, mark-men, men of the assay,
you weighed him at the ford and found him light.
Weigh your grief. It will come up short.*

The envoy straightened slowly. Behind her the frozen clods knocked down onto the lid.

questions.rec_reason: It sets the Eastern court's poem exchange and the Northern verse duel side by side, so the blend shows in the talk itself and each culture answers in its own form.

questions.title: Long formal speech and the clipped line
questions.question: How long may a speaker hold the floor: formal argument at court, short lines in the north, or length wherever the moment carries it?
questions.context: This reopens R48-43, ruled 2026-09-26: 'one crafted, eloquent speech at a big moment'; R52-06-TRIADS already makes 'parallel clauses' legal 'in any mouth'. Chinese court and council scenes run long formal argument in matched clauses, and wuxia (Chinese martial-hero fiction) villains boast at length; the sagas and the Kharven speak in short declaratives.

options.label: One speech per scene
options.consequence: R48-43 stands: dialogue stays realistic and short under pressure, and one trained speaker gets one crafted speech at a big moment.
options.sample: "The hall has grain and the Seat has the road," Envoy Shen said. "You need the one and we need the other. I don't see much here to argue." He waited. Nobody spoke. The clan chief turned his cup on the table a quarter turn and back. Smoke from the blubber lamp hung under the roof-beam, and somewhere outside a man was splitting rounds for the woodpile, steady as a clock. "You'll take the skin first," the chief said, and pushed the sealskin across.

options.label: Long speech at court
options.consequence: Court cultures (the Moto court, the Accord chancery, the Mahuo houses, the lineage halls) argue in long formal speeches as their normal register; Kharven, saga and soldier speech stay short. R48-43's cap holds outside court.
options.sample: Envoy Shen rose, set both hands flat on the table, and spoke as a hall speaks before a throne. "The hall has grain and no road. The Seat has the road and no grain. A granary without a road feeds rats; a road without a granary carries only the dead. My master asks the Seat to count. Count the winters since the grass went. Count the bowls. Count the children who reached the spring, and the ones who lay in the death-house through the Thin Weeks." The clan chief turned his cup a quarter turn and back. "You'll take the skin first," he said.

options.label: Long speech anywhere earned
options.consequence: Anyone may hold the floor at length when the moment carries it: council, challenge, boast, lament. R48-43's cap is struck; R19-4-REALISTIC_SPEECH ('Speech is not prose') still governs the frightened.
