options.sample: Envoy Shen rose and laid it out in the hall's long manner: grain and no road, road and no grain, the winters counted, the children counted. The clan chief heard him to the end. Then he stood, and the hall went quiet, because he did not often stand. "Count, he says. My grandfather rode to Muken with forty horses and came home with nine, and he never asked a stranger to count them for him. We counted the grass when it went. We counted our dead into the cold. Your master may keep his abacus. You'll take the skin first."

questions.rec_reason: Keying length to culture makes the courts sound like courts and the north sound like the north, which is the Eastern court tradition and the saga tradition each in its own room.

questions.title: Face, and the face-slap
questions.question: Does face run as a social economy in speech, and is the public reversal of an arrogant man (the face-slap) a legal payoff?
questions.context: Face is public standing, given, saved or lost before witnesses. Chinese web fiction runs on it: an arrogant scion humiliates a hidden-strength hero, who reverses it in public (the face-slap, paid off as shuang, the reader's rush of satisfaction). WOTR's NPCs are 'never omniscient, never dumb' (R48-36), and only those with 'the standing to be arrogant' may gloat (R12-4-VOICE_THREE_OPPONENT).

options.label: Face unnamed, as now
options.consequence: No rule is written: status shows in bows, seats and the order of speech; nobody names face, and no scene is built around a humiliation reversed.
options.sample: Lu Pei came in out of the snow with four of his father's men behind him and took the seat nearest the brazier, which was the master's. The hall went on eating. Old Master Lu finished his broth, set the bowl down, and asked after the boy's father's health, in full, by every title the man held. It took some time. When it was done Lu Pei was the only one in the hall still sitting, and he stood.

options.label: Face as currency
options.consequence: Face becomes a named social economy, given, saved, borrowed and owed in speech and tracked like a Ledger debt. Humiliators stay clever (R48-36); there is no ritual reversal payoff.
options.sample: "You give me no face, uncle," Lu Pei said, and took the seat nearest the brazier. The hall went on eating. Old Master Lu finished his broth. "I gave your father face for thirty years," he said. "He spent it. You came here to borrow against his account." He set the bowl down. "Sit, then. I'll lend you this much: nobody here will say what they saw. Tomorrow you'll owe me for their silence." Lu Pei sat. Every man at the table had heard the price.

options.label: The face-slap licensed
options.consequence: The face-slap becomes a legal payoff: an arrogant scion underestimates, the reversal is public, the room reassesses. R5-C1-WELL_REASONED_WRONG_CONCLUSION and R48-36 relax for the arrogant, who may misjudge badly.
options.sample: "Old man, your hall is a kennel," Lu Pei said, and took the seat nearest the brazier. One of his father's men laughed. Old Master Lu finished his broth, set the bowl down, and flicked the spoon. It took the laughing man in the throat under the jaw, and he sat down hard by the door with his mouth working and no air coming in. Lu Pei looked at the spoon in the snow, and at the old man's hands, and got up out of the master's seat with his face gone the colour of the coals.

options.label: The face-slap, with a bill
options.consequence: C, with a bill: every public reversal opens a Front or a Ledger debt (a vengeful house, a witness, a feud), and the humbled man stays veteran-clever afterward.
options.sample: "Old man, your hall is a kennel," Lu Pei said, and took the master's seat. One of his men laughed. Old Master Lu flicked his spoon. It took the laughing man under the jaw, and he sat down by the door with his mouth working and no air coming in. Lu Pei got up out of the seat with his face gone the colour of the coals. That night a rider left for the Lu hall in the south carrying the dead man's name, the price of a funeral, and the old master's name written underneath, twice.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the strongest pleasure of Chinese web fiction and makes it pay grimdark rent: the reversal lands, and the world sends the invoice.

sections.title: Humour and tone
sections.intro: What makes WOTR funny, warm or wet-eyed under the blend. Gallows wit survives every option; the questions are what joins it.

questions.title: The double act and the comic beat
questions.question: Does the setup-deadpan-reaction ban hold, or may a comic double act play out on the page?
questions.context: R5-D-HUMOUR_BARRED bars 'the beat structure of setup, deadpan and reaction', and R52-31 (ruled 2026-09-26) allows comic NPCs only without it. Japanese manzai comedy is a double act: the boke (the fool) says something absurd and the tsukkomi (the straight man) cuts him down, often with a smack; manga add the gag reaction, an exaggerated body response.

options.label: The ban holds
options.consequence: R5-D-HUMOUR_BARRED stands: no comic beat is built to land; humour arrives in talk already moving and never pauses the scene. Comic NPCs keep R52-31's limit.
options.sample: "I can smell a Well-spawn at a mile," Dunn said, sniffing at the wind as they walked the wagons down to the ford. "Hot pennies and wet dog." "That's the mule," Garside said, without turning round. "You've been smelling the mule since the last post-house." Dunn sniffed again. Ahead of them the ice at the ford's edge was broken in a wide ring, from beneath, and the wagon horses had begun to balk.

options.label: Double act in dialogue
options.consequence: The fool-and-straight-man exchange becomes legal in dialogue for anyone; narration may not stop for a reaction. R5-D's bar narrows to narrated beats.
options.sample: "I can smell a Well-spawn at a mile," Dunn said. "Hot pennies and wet dog." "That's the mule." "The mule smells of mule. This is under the mule." "Under the mule is also the mule." "I've a gift, Garside." "You've a nose like a cellar door and a head to match. Walk." Dunn walked, sniffing. Ahead of them the ice at the ford's edge was broken in a wide ring, from beneath.

options.label: Full comic beats
options.consequence: R5-D-HUMOUR_BARRED and R5-G's comedic-beat tell are struck: setup, retort and a narrated physical reaction (the cuff, the gaping pause) are legal wherever a scene can carry them.
options.sample: "I can smell a Well-spawn at a mile," Dunn said, nose up into the wind like a hound at a kitchen door. "Hot pennies and wet dog." Garside let three full paces go by. Then he reached over and cuffed him across the back of the head, hard enough to tip his hat into the snow. "That's the mule, you article." Dunn stood with his hat in his hand and his mouth open. He sniffed at the mule. At the air. At the mule again. Ahead of them the ice at the ford's edge was broken in a wide ring, from beneath.

options.label: Full beats for comic voices
options.consequence: Full comic beats, retort and reaction included, belong to comic voices and double acts named on their cards; everyone else stays under R5-D.
options.sample: "I can smell a Well-spawn at a mile," Dunn said, nose up into the wind. "Hot pennies and wet dog." Garside let three full paces go by, then cuffed him across the back of the head hard enough to tip his hat into the snow. "That's the mule, you article." Dunn stood sniffing at the mule, the air, the mule again. At the head of the line the wagon-master never turned round. He had seen the ring in the ice at the ford's edge, broken from beneath. He was easing the shotgun out of its boot.

questions.rec_reason: It gives the manzai double act and the gag beat to the people built for them and keeps the grim cast clean, so the comedy sharpens the danger beside it.

questions.title: Grimdark and warmth
questions.question: How much warmth does WOTR carry beside the grimdark: bonds, found family, hope?
questions.context: NATALIE.md says victories cost and 'Hope is small and hard-won'; R11-1-TONAL_SPINE_UNCHANGED keeps Pack Five's tonal spine. Progression fantasy is an optimistic climb; shōnen (Japanese action comics for boys) and murim (Korean martial-world fiction) run on found family and loyalty; cultivation novels (Chinese fantasy of climbing realms of inner power) on master and disciple. The house prose today is grief, cost and dry wit, with joy and wonder rare.

options.label: Grimdark spine, as now
options.consequence: NATALIE.md's grimdark line and R11-1 stand: warmth is small and paid for, joy is rare, and most scenes end on a cost.

options.label: Warmth as counterweight
options.consequence: Each live thread carries at least one standing warm bond (found family, master and disciple, sworn kin) written openly warm, and joy may get scenes of its own. Losses still cost.

options.label: Even split, hope can grow
options.consequence: Warm and grim scenes run in rough balance; hope may grow across an arc, and the POV's progression is a real climb with real wins, though the world stays dangerous.

options.label: Tone set per thread
options.consequence: Tone is set per thread on its State of Play (the Kharven war grim, an academy thread warmer), and a thread may shift when the story earns it.

questions.rec_reason: Warmth gives grief something to take; the Eastern bonds of master, disciple, sworn kin and house are the blend's best gift to tone, and the costs still land.

questions.title: Tears and sentiment
questions.question: When a guarded character breaks, how openly does the page let them cry?
questions.context: R52-26-GRIEF takes a voice 'back to its root', and R49-07 says to 'show it in the body first'. Shōnen heroes and Korean drama let strong men weep openly at a bond's peak; han (Korean grief held for years) breaks at a small trigger after long restraint; Japanese literary restraint, as in Kawabata, leaves before the tears. IN3 covers how feeling is carried.

options.label: Held, as now
options.consequence: R49-07 and R52-28-COMPOSURE stand: a guarded character's grief shows in hands, breath and what they do; open weeping is rare and small.
options.sample: The old rider sat the Waiting for his son with the rest of them, back straight, hands on his knees, through the night. When the women brought out the boy's things he took the belt and turned it over once. It was worn soft where the hand goes. His fingers found the place. They stayed there. His breath went out white, came back short, went out again. In the morning he gave the belt to his grandson and went to split wood.

options.label: Break at a small thing
options.consequence: A rule adds the delayed break: restraint holds through the big moment and gives way, fully and openly, at a small unexpected thing. Once per character per arc.
options.sample: The old rider sat the Waiting for his son with the rest of them, back straight, hands on his knees, through the night. When the women brought out the boy's things he turned the belt over once and handed it on. He made no sound. It was the bowl that broke him. Someone had set out the boy's bowl for the morning broth, from habit, and the old man saw the chip in its rim the boy had made at six. He put his face in his hands in front of the whole death-house and wept aloud. The women came.

options.label: Open tears at the bond
options.consequence: Strong characters may weep openly at a bond's peaks (a death, a reunion, a teacher's praise), in front of others, and the room may answer it.
options.sample: The old rider sat the Waiting for his son with the rest of them, and when the women brought out the boy's belt he took it in both hands and wept over it openly, and left his face unwiped. "He held the ford," he said, to the room, to the dead. "He held it till the horses came. My boy held it." The tears ran into his beard and froze there. Across the death-house the other riders stood, one by one, and put their fists to their chests.

options.label: Cut away before the break
options.consequence: Restraint goes further: the scene leaves before the break, and the reader gets only what it left behind (frost in a beard, a barred door).
options.sample: The old rider sat the Waiting for his son with the rest of them, back straight, hands on his knees, through the night. When the women brought out the boy's things he took the belt and turned it over once. Then he stood. "I'll see to the horses." He went out into the dark. In the morning the grandson found the stable door barred from inside and waited by it a long time. When the old man came out, the front of his beard was stiff with frost, and the boy's belt was buckled round his own coat.

questions.rec_reason: It is the han shape and suits WOTR's guarded cast: the restraint the law already writes becomes the setup for one break that lands harder for coming late.

questions.title: Comedy beside danger
questions.question: May a comic beat sit inside real danger, or hard against it?
questions.context: R5-B-MANHWA_DIRECTIVE_REPEALED lists absurdist comedy beside real stakes as a tell; R5-D-HUMOUR_PERMITTED allows gallows wit 'from people whose profession earns it' and 'the joke that is also a threat'. Shōnen and murim drop a gag into a deadly fight; Lord of the Mysteries, already a named WOTR model, sets horror hard after domestic comedy.

options.label: Gallows wit only, as now
options.consequence: R5-B and R5-D stand: inside real danger the only humour is gallows wit and the joke that is a threat, from someone whose work has earned it.
options.sample: The flusher had his lamp turned down to a bead and his back against the wet brick. "Lad," he said, very low. "If it takes me first, my debts are yours. Four silver at the gin-shop on Tanner's Row, and mind you pay it. They've long memories." The boy did not laugh. Down the culvert, past the reach of the lamp, the water changed its note, as if something wide had stepped into it, and stopped.

options.label: A comic beat mid-danger
options.consequence: A short comic beat may break inside a fight or crisis (a pratfall, an absurd turn) so long as the danger is unchanged when it ends; R5-B's absurdism tell narrows to beats that defuse the danger.
options.sample: Down the culvert something wide stepped into the water. The flusher raised his lamp, and the thing raised its head into the light, and it was a sow, an ordinary grey sow plastered in sewer muck and furious, and she came straight between the boy's legs and dumped him flat in the run-off. The flusher laughed so hard he had to hold the wall. Then he stopped laughing. Behind the sow, at the edge of the lamp, something taller stood in the water, and it had been driving her.

options.label: Comedy hard against dread
options.consequence: Comedy and dread may be set hard against each other by design (domestic farce, then the thing in the dark), each played straight; jokes inside the danger stay gallows wit.
options.sample: At supper the flusher's wife had made him wear the new collar to the culvert in case the Board man came, and he had argued it all through the pie. "It's starched, woman. I'll be strangled." "Then you'll be strangled clean." The boy had laughed till gravy came down his nose. Now the collar was black with sewer water and the flusher stood very still with his lamp turned down to a bead, because down the culvert something wide had stepped into the run and stopped, and it was breathing.

questions.rec_reason: It is the Lord of the Mysteries move WOTR already names as a model: the comedy makes the dread land harder, and the fight itself stays deadly.

sections.title: Names, titles and epithets in narration
sections.intro: What the world calls people, and what the narration calls them. How narration varies an epithet inside a scene is VO4's question; these settle sobriquets, hall titles and honorifics.

questions.title: Sobriquets and hall titles
questions.question: How freely does the world hand out grand names, and may the lineage halls run title ladders?
questions.context: R20-4-THIRD_NAME_PROBLEM makes the Third Name 'the earned title that the world assigns', and R50-21 lets an NPC coin one for your characters, kept only if you keep it. Wuxia and murim (Chinese and Korean martial fiction) hang a sobriquet on every notable fighter and run sect title ladders; R23-10-CHINESE_PHONOTACTICS bans 'sect-title constructions' and 'honorific stacking'.

options.label: Third Names only, as now
options.consequence: R20-4, R50-21 and R23-10 stand: one earned Third Name for those whose deeds made one; the halls use plain kin and teaching titles, never stacked.
options.sample: The gate-clerk read the delegation off the hall's own letter: Master Shen of the Shen lineage hall, his nephew, two students, four servants, six mules. He read it in the voice he kept for salt manifests. On the wall the clansmen counted the mules. They lost interest. The thin old man on the lead mule kept his hands in his sleeves and studied the dark old courses at the base of the gate, as if he were pricing them.

options.label: Sobriquets in common use
options.consequence: Criers, crowds, ballads and enemies may hang lesser names on any notable fighter; most fade, and the one that sticks becomes the Third Name. Your characters' names still stick only if you keep them.
options.sample: The gate-clerk read the delegation off the hall's own letter, and the crier took it up for the yard. "Shen Guowei, called the Quiet Abacus, who broke the salt market at Hallenfeld with a counting-board and never drew steel!" The yard knew the name. Men came out of the smithy to look, the farrier with a shoe still in his tongs. The thin old man on the lead mule kept his hands in his sleeves. He let them look.

options.label: Hall title ladders
options.consequence: The lineage halls run a full title ladder (Hall Master, Elder, Senior Brother, first disciple) that may stack in formal address; R23-10's bans lift for titles and hold for given names.
options.sample: The gate-clerk read the delegation off the hall's own letter, and the crier took it up for the yard. "Hall Master Shen Guowei, Third Elder of the Shen lineage hall!" Then the nephew: "Senior Brother Shen Lian, first disciple of the Hall Master!" Then the two students, by generation, junior to junior. It took a while. The yard counted the titles under its breath, and the thin old man on the lead mule kept his hands in his sleeves while they were read.

options.label: Sobriquets and title ladders
options.consequence: B and C together: sobriquets spread by use, and the halls stack their titles in formal address. R23-10 holds for given names only.
options.sample: The gate-clerk read the delegation off the hall's own letter, and the crier took it up for the yard. "Hall Master Shen Guowei, Third Elder of the Shen lineage hall, called the Quiet Abacus, who broke the salt market at Hallenfeld and never drew steel!" Then the nephew, Senior Brother Shen Lian, first disciple of the Hall Master. It took a while. Men came out of the smithy to look. The thin old man on the lead mule kept his hands in his sleeves and let them.

questions.rec_reason: Sobriquets are how the martial world keeps score in public and title ladders are the halls' heraldry; the Third Name stays the one that sticks, and R23-10 still keeps Chinese given names apart from the Korean stratum.

questions.title: Honorifics in narration
questions.question: In narration, do Eastern-register characters go by name, by rank, or with the honorific the POV would use?
questions.context: R48-44 (ruled 2026-09-26) names characters 'the way the viewpoint sees them', and R20-5-ON_THE_PAGE introduces them 'by whatever name the POV character would use'; honorifics are law in Japonic speech (R51-21) and unruled in narration. Japanese and Chinese narration often names a lord by office and a teacher by title; Western close third uses the given name.

options.label: Plain names, as now
options.consequence: Narration uses the name or epithet the POV would use, in plain form, with no honorific suffixes; honorifics live in speech (R51-21).
options.sample: Old Tobe had served the Shirogane forty winters. When Kaname came in off the yard with blood on his sleeve, Tobe took the sword from him and turned it in the lamplight, reading the edge for nicks. Kaname stood over him while he read it. "His," Kaname said, of the blood. Tobe nodded. He went for the paper and the oil, and when he came back Kaname was asleep sitting up, as his father used to sleep after a duel.

options.label: By rank and place
options.consequence: Narration names Eastern-register characters by their culture's custom whatever the POV: Japonic houses by office or place in the house, hall members by title and family name.
options.sample: Old Tobe had served the Shirogane forty winters. When the second son came in off the yard with blood on his sleeve, Tobe took the sword from him and turned it in the lamplight, reading the edge for nicks. The second son stood over him while he read it. "His," the second son said, of the blood. Tobe nodded. He went for the paper and the oil, and when he came back the young lord was asleep sitting up, as his father used to sleep after a duel.

options.label: The POV's own honorific
options.consequence: A close POV from a culture with honorifics carries them into narration (Kaname-sama, Seo-nim) as he would think them, never italic; a Western POV in the same room uses plain names.
options.sample: Old Tobe had served the Shirogane forty winters. When Kaname-sama came in off the yard with blood on his sleeve, Tobe took the sword from him and turned it in the lamplight, reading the edge for nicks. Kaname-sama stood over him while he read it. "His," he said, of the blood. Tobe nodded. He went for the paper and the oil, and when he came back Kaname-sama was asleep sitting up, as his father used to sleep after a duel.

questions.rec_reason: It brings Eastern address into the narration through close POV, where R48-44 already wants the naming to characterise, and a Western POV in the same scene shows the gap between the two.

sections.title: Names: comic, punning and made names
sections.intro: How many of WOTR's names carry a joke, which kinds, who carries them, and whether the world or only the reader hears it. Your PC and the other creators' characters sit outside every option here.

questions.title: How much of the pool is comic
questions.question: What share of new names should be comic, punning or plainly made-up fantasy names?
questions.context: R50-18 dropped the old outlier budget (a cap on names that fit no naming stratum): outliers are now 'free, no ratio, no reason needed'. The struck R23-5 had warned that past its ratio, names read as 'an author picking names he liked'.

options.label: A seasoning
options.consequence: About one comic name in a crowd scene, usually a nickname among the commons. Nearly every other new name stays strict to its bank (a culture's list of name parts).
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat, his breath standing white in front of each name. Aldric Hale. Ralf Osterby. Dunstan Fenn. Kettle. A short sealer in a hide-coat stepped out at that one, and the column laughed, low, the way men laughed in that cold. The sergeant did not look up. Greta Coll. Nella Ashby. Fern Tolley. The wind came off the rock and took the rest of the laughter with it.

options.label: Most commons and soldiers
options.consequence: Comic bynames and nicknames become the norm in musters, crews, taverns and markets. Above the commons they thin out, and NM4 sets how high they reach.
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat, his breath standing white in front of each name. Aldric Two-Bowls. Ralf Wetfoot. Dunstan the Lesser, whose brother had been Dunstan the Least. Kettle. Fern Halfpenny. Hob and Dob Garth, who answered together. Nobody in the column laughed. They had heard the roll every morning since the thaw, and the only name that still made a sound among them was the one he skipped.

options.label: About a third
options.consequence: Roughly one new name in three carries a joke, spread across every rank NM4 opens. The rest follow their banks.
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat, his breath standing white in front of each name. Captain Edric Pinchgauge, on the grey. Aldric Hale. Ralf Wetfoot. Dunstan Fenn. Kettle. Nella Coll. Hob and Dob Garth, who answered together. The captain heard his own name read out in the cold and touched his hat to it, as his father had, and his grandfather, who had at least been a gauger.

options.label: Pratchett density
options.consequence: Most new names carry a joke, as in Discworld, and a strict bank name becomes the exception. Comedy reads as the world's own habit.
options.sample: The sergeant read the roll off a slate at the gate of the Seat. Captain Edric Pinchgauge, on the grey. Aldric Drinkwater. Ralf Wetfoot. Dunstan Gotobed. Kettle. Fern Halfpenny. Nella Breakseal. Hob and Dob Garth, together. Last came Snorin, a Dawi cooper who had signed on for the pay and was asleep on his feet between the shafts of the supply sledge, and the sergeant read his name twice before the man beside him kicked his ankle.

questions.rec_reason: It answers your 'a lot' where the commons live, which is where Norse bynames and English phrase surnames grew in fact, and leaves the reach up the cast to NM4.

questions.title: Built comic names
questions.question: Which kinds of built comic name should WOTR use?
questions.context: R50-17 lets characters 'sound alike', and when they meet 'it becomes a beat'. The Dvergatal, the dwarf-list in the Norse poem Völuspá that Tolkien mined, chimes Fíli with Kíli. Dickens built surnames one notch past believable (Gradgrind), and real English surnames run as odd (Gotobed, Drinkwater).

options.label: Rhyming and alliterating sets
options.consequence: Kin, crews and sworn pairs share a name-part and change the sound, Borin and Snorin style, inside each culture's own sound rules. A set meeting is a beat (R50-17).
options.sample:
Halrin, Kalrin and Valtrin: Kegshard cooper brothers on the shared Dawi element Rin (cut).
Hob and Dob Garth: Northern twins christened with one name, told apart by its two pet forms.
Lu Anping and Lu Anning: lineage-hall cousins sharing the generation syllable An (peace), as the family poem required.

options.label: Dickensian talking surnames
options.consequence: Surnames that tell a trade or a nature one notch past believable, as Gradgrind did: the Victorian imperial register R53-28 already sets, for Northern and Accord families.
options.sample:
Keva Pinchgauge: a Guild inspector whose readings always came out a hair under the meter.
Penn Shortloaf: a baker from a family fined under the assize so often that the fine became the name.
Calla Quillfast: a registry clerk, never once slow.

options.label: Plausible puns, Pratchett-style
options.consequence: Surnames that pass for real ones, with the pun underneath or turned against the bearer. Built from words the Draw Age owns, so no brand, celebrity or modern-world reference.
options.sample:
Niall Lightfoot: a courier with a ruined knee, still the fastest on the Seat road.
Edric Spendlove: a Guild paymaster who never rounded a sum up.
Ivor Drinkwater: sergeant of the driest column in the north, by his own order.

options.label: Phrase and sentence names
options.consequence: A verb and its object frozen into a surname (Shakespeare, Gotobed), and a sect that names its children as moral sentences, as the Puritans did (Sorry-for-sin).
options.sample:
The Breakseals: three generations of honest gaugers, searched at every gate for the name.
Kit Burnoil: of commons who never held a draw licence and said so.
Abide-the-Measure Coll: a child of a strict Guild sect, called Bide by everyone who shared her bunk.

questions.rec_reason: Sets, talking surnames and plausible puns all grow from real naming custom and hold up in a grim room. Sentence names tell the reader what to think of a person on entrance, and the best phrase surnames arrive anyway under C.

questions.title: Grown comic names
questions.question: Which kinds of comic name that grow out of use should WOTR use?
questions.context: A byname is a second name others give for a trade, a look or a deed. R23-2 makes one 'available to anyone' in the Northern stratum, and the naming amendment's Far-Northern section calls bynames 'freely coined'. R50-33 spells a foreigner's bent version of a name 'as heard in dialogue'.

options.label: Soldiers' nicknames
options.consequence: Deed and body bynames from comrades, literal or ironic, the way Abercrombie's Logen Ninefingers counts his missing finger. Peers coin them, so the joke belongs to the characters.
options.sample:
Haldor Two-Bowls: took a second bowl in the Thin Weeks; the laughter stopped when he walked in.
Kitten: the biggest man on the Seat's wall, named by men who later stopped saying it to his face.
Kalvak Twelvecasks: a Dawi cooper; the twelve were the casks he soured.

options.label: Mangled names
options.consequence: A name or phrase bent by a foreign mouth and written as heard, a real mishearing every time (R20-4). Canon already does it: the Dawi say Porin, and Common mouths make it Borin.
options.sample:
Borin: every Common mouth's version of Porin, the softened stops the Dawi call 'voiced', careless speech.
Solly Transit: the Kharven riders' name for any Accord gate clerk, from his 'Solutum et transitum' (paid and passed).
Kettle: a sealer the survey clerk entered by the pot in his hands.

options.label: Sound comedy
options.consequence: Names funny for their noise: hard k sounds, doubled syllables, a goblin mouth's extra consonants. Built inside each people's own sound rules, and most at home among the goblinoids.
options.sample:
Gorrgorr: a goblin porter; gorr is Old Vaross (the goblin tongue) for a load borne, and he bore two.
Gripsnick and Gripsnack: goblin sapper twins, spelled differently by every clerk who met them.
Ukkukk: 'one-one', a goblin fence who always had exactly one left.

options.label: Protective ugly names
options.consequence: A child given a cheap or ugly name so death passes it over, as Chinese and Korean families did; R23-5 already allows a name given 'as an insult or a shield'. Comic to outsiders, grim at home.
options.sample:
Wet Wood: a sickly Kharven girl's name through her first winter, an insult for the cold to hear and a promise for her mother, since wet wood burns eventually.
Gousheng: 'dog's leftovers', a hall elder's milk-name, which his sister still used at seventy in front of the whole hall.

questions.rec_reason: Each grows inside the world out of someone's mouth or custom, so every joke has an owner, which keeps it out of the narration's mouth.

questions.title: Who may carry one
questions.question: How far up the cast may a comic name reach?
questions.context: R52-31 allows 'a comic minor NPC as a comic voice from the start', and R5-D permits 'the joke that is also a threat'. Your PC and the other creators' characters sit outside every option here; that is settled.

options.label: Walk-ons and commons
options.consequence: Comic names stay with one-scene people, crowds, musters and markets. Anyone who recurs gets a strict name.
options.sample:
Dry Tom: a ferryman met once at the ford.
Hob and Dob Garth: two lines on one muster roll.
Kettle: a sealer at a survey post, never seen again.

options.label: Plus recurring NPCs
options.consequence: Recurring minor NPCs (the innkeeper, the sergeant, the Guild clerk) may keep comic names across scenes. Villains and major NPCs stay strict.
options.sample:
Sergeant Ivor Drinkwater: the same dry sergeant through a whole campaign.
Mother Gristle: sold windmeat at the Seat's lower gate on every visit.
Keva Pinchgauge: at every gauge-housing she inspected.

options.label: Plus villains
options.consequence: B, plus villains and rivals, in the Jonson and Dickens line (Volpone the fox, Uriah Heep): a comic name on a dangerous person. Major NPCs keep strict names.
options.sample:
Magister Aulus Tardipes: 'slow-foot' in correct Latin, who signed every death warrant late and never once in error.
Niall Pennywhistle: a Guild factor who bought a district's draw for a song and sold it back by the cup.

options.label: Any rank Natalie makes
options.consequence: Any character Natalie creates, major NPCs included, may carry a comic name. Your PC and the other creators' characters never do.
options.sample:
Halfpint: a Banner House heir his own men named, carrying a full arc.
Old Fumble: a Measurewright across three books, the best reader of Crystals in the north.

questions.rec_reason: A dangerous man with a comic name is the oldest English stage trick and grimdark's best use of the joke that is also a threat; strict names on major NPCs keep the story's weight where it sits.

questions.title: Whose ear hears the joke
questions.question: Must a comic name be a joke someone inside the world can hear, or may some be the reader's alone?
questions.context: R5-C1: 'The narration never winks.' Common, the shared trade tongue, is what the page writes as English, so an English pun is heard in a Common mouth; one buried in a Dawi or Moto name reaches the reader alone. R50-01 makes real-language names 'real, correct phrases'.

options.label: In-world jokes only
options.consequence: Every comic name is funny in its bearer's own tongue or in a Common mouth, and a character glosses it once (says its meaning aloud). Snorin exists only as a Common nickname.
options.sample: The Dawi set his hands flat on the Guild counter and gave his name in his own tongue, Halrin Tharnsson, hard and clean, as if the clerk were auditing him. The clerk wrote it down and thought it sounded noble. Behind the Dawi his foreman laughed into his beard. "The hold calls him Kurlo," he told the clerk, in Common. "Unbegun. It's what he says to every job he's given. Put him on the night casks."

options.label: English puns with a bridge
options.consequence: An English pun is legal where the world supplies a bridge: a Common mouth, a byname rendered in English, or a Common ear mishearing. Reader-only puns hidden in a foreign name stay out.
options.sample: The Dawi set his hands flat on the Guild counter and gave his name in his own tongue, hard and clean, as if the clerk were auditing him. The clerk had not caught a syllable of it. Behind the Dawi the night foreman was already laughing. "Put him down as Snorin," he said. "Everyone does. Sleeps on the cask-stack between shifts." The Dawi did not know the word. He watched the clerk write it in the Concord hand and nodded, gravely, at his new name.

options.label: English puns anywhere
options.consequence: Any name may carry an English pun, foreign given names included (Snorin as a Dawi's own name, an outlier under R50-18). The reader hears it and the characters may not. R5-C1 narrows to narrated remarks.
options.sample: The Dawi set his hands flat on the Guild counter. "Snorin Kalrinsson," he said, hard and clean, as if the clerk were auditing him. The clerk wrote it in the Concord hand and asked for his hold. Kegshard, said Snorin. Cooper. Twelve years on the night casks. Behind him the queue shuffled and coughed in the cold of the hall. The clerk blotted the line, slid the token across, and called the next man.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the no-wink rule, gives you your Snorin today in any Common mouth, and lets the Dawi's own gravity become part of the joke.

questions.title: Which peoples: West and North
questions.question: Among the Dawi, the northern peoples and the goblinoids, which carry comic names?
questions.context: Most peoples already have a comic slot: Northern bynames 'available to anyone' (R23-2), goblinoid bynames 'describing the force that made the person' (R20-1). Dawi given names come from a fixed thirty-element bank (R20-3), and the Dawi call Common's softened stops (Borin for Porin) careless speech.

options.label: The Dawi
options.consequence: Rhyming sets on a shared bank element, deed bynames rendered in English, and outsiders' mangling. Given names stay bank-built; the joke lives in sets, bynames and other people's mouths.
options.sample:
Valtgrim, Kalgrim and Holmgrim: a mining crew on the shared element Grim (forge), the Grims to every foreman.
Kalvak Twelvecasks: the hold entered the soured casks with a straight face.
Bare-chin: canon's Dawi insult for a beard with no rings, no time served.

options.label: Kharven and Far-Northern
options.consequence: Bynames from the Kharven stock of scarcity insults, protective cheap names, and roll-names (surnames an Accord clerk assigned). No joke on the name of the recently dead (R23-11).
options.sample:
Haldor Two-Bowls: the second bowl in the Thin Weeks.
Short-Stack: a lazy man's byname, coined by the neighbours who kept his fire lit.
Bucket: a roll-name a clerk took off the thing in a sealer's hands, paid in tax for three generations.

options.label: Accord and Northern commons
options.consequence: The richest home: talking and phrase surnames, rhyming pet names (Hob and Dob), soldiers' bynames, and Accord jokes in correct Latin (R50-12).
options.sample:
Keva Pinchgauge: a Guild inspector who read light.
Hob and Dob Garth: two pet forms of one name on one roll.
Magister Aulus Tardipes: 'slow-foot' in correct Latin, inspector of couriers.

options.label: Goblinoid peoples
options.consequence: Sound comedy, and bynames whose cause nobody remembers, so a dreaded name can arrive with no story behind it.
options.sample:
Gorrgorr: 'load-load', a porter who carried double.
Gripsnick and Gripsnack: sapper twins.
Grinmaw the Unexplained: feared through three districts, for reasons nobody alive could give.

questions.rec_reason: Each people already has a native comic slot, so the jokes grow from custom. The Dawi keep their given names grave and take their comedy in sets, bynames and other people's mouths.

questions.title: Which peoples: the Eastern strata
questions.question: Among the Japonic houses, the Mahuo and the Chinese lineage halls, which carry comic names?
questions.context: The Japonic houses keep a 'name-taboo on the living' (R23-2), so retainers already go by calling-names, and a Moto given name 'states what the line expects' (R40-1). Names show 'romanised only' (R50-31), so a pun needing written characters never reaches the page. Canon holds one sound pun already: Daigo Tenryū, the Dango Dragon (dango: a rice dumpling).

options.label: Retainers and household staff
options.consequence: Retainers and servants of the Japonic houses take calling-names from real Japanese trait-words, and sound puns on real words, glossed once by a character.
options.sample:
Nebosuke: a gate sentry; the -suke ending made 'sleepyhead' sound like a boy's name.
Kuishinbō: a cook's boy, 'glutton', worn as a calling-name.
The Dango Dragon: canon's own sound pun, on Daigo Tenryū.

options.label: Bloodline cadets, bynames only
options.consequence: Servants and rival Lines coin comic bynames for new cadets of the archaic houses, behind their backs; given names stay under R40-1. No carded Moto is touched, Sodoku least of all, and no Büri form returns.
options.sample:
Lord Lantern: the Shirogane servants' name for a cadet lord nobody saw by day.
Old Inkstone: a Yuno archivist's name in the kitchen, never above stairs.

options.label: The Mahuo
options.consequence: Korean-register names chime through the generation syllable (one syllable every cousin of a generation shares) and can land on a real Korean word; children may carry ugly milk-names. Real Korean only (R50-01).
options.sample:
Dae-chang: 'great prosperity' from the house bank, and the market's word for grilled beef tripe; his cousins all shared the Dae.
Ju-jeong: 'sovereign, correct', said exactly like the Korean for a drunk's rambling.
Gaettong-i: 'dog dung', a Mahuo heir's milk-name, kept now only by his old nurse.

options.label: The Chinese lineage halls
options.consequence: Self-awarded studio names (a scholar's chosen art-name, which other houses mock), insulting posthumous names, cheap child-names and spoken homophone puns. Nothing that needs a written character to land.
options.sample:
Fantong: 'rice bucket', a useless eater's nickname, once written on a Concord contract as a cook's legal name.
Jiuyun Zhai: 'Studio of Nine Clouds', the name an alchemist awarded himself; other halls said Nine Clouds once he left the room.
Gu Huan: 'Gu the Slow', a physician's posthumous name in the hall book, for arriving late at every death.

questions.rec_reason: Each stratum has a real comic custom to draw on. B keeps the ruling houses' given names grave and makes the servants pay for the joke in whispers, which is the joke that is also a threat.

questions.title: Borin Ironheart's rhyming kin
questions.question: Should Borin Ironheart gain a rhyming set of kin or companions, and who makes them?
questions.context: Borin's card names no kin, patronymic (father's name) or oath-name, and says he 'Tells terrible jokes and laughs at them himself'. His name parses from the Dawi bank as Bor (carry) plus Rin (cut), so rhymes on Rin are legal Dawi; Snorin fits no bank element and works only in Common.

options.label: No kin, rhymes elsewhere
options.consequence: Borin's card stays as written. Rhyming Dawi sets appear among new characters, and any set that meets Borin is a beat (R50-17).
options.sample:
Halrin, Kalrin and Valtrin: unrelated Kegshard coopers, whom Borin greeted as long-lost cousins to annoy them.
Borin: unchanged on his card, still laughing at the cooper joke before the punchline.

options.label: Brothers, Snorin included
options.consequence: Natalie invents Borin's brothers on the shared Rin, one called Snorin by every Common mouth, and adds them to his card's kin line once you approve the names.
options.sample:
Torin: the eldest, a hold-reeve (a hold's steward) who had not laughed at one of Borin's jokes in three centuries.
Kalrin: the youngest, a cooper who slept on the cask-stacks, Snorin to every Accord buyer.
Borin: the middle brother, who started the nickname.

options.label: A rhyming forge crew
options.consequence: The Soul Forge's journeymen become a rhyming crew, the Dvergatal habit of chiming companies, and Borin's family stays unwritten. Snorin is the crew's sleeper.
options.sample:
Ymir Rhok: still Borin's Whetstone, outside the rhyme.
Halrin, Valtrin and Kalrin: the night crew at the Soul Forge.
Snorin: what the Accord buyers called Kalrin, who slept on the charcoal sacks.

options.label: You pick from three
options.consequence: Natalie pitches three sets in chat (kin, forge crew, rival smiths), and nothing reaches the card or the page until you pick one.
options.sample:
Set one: brothers on Rin.
Set two: a forge crew on Rin and Grim.
Set three: a rival hold's rhyming smiths, who mocked his jokes.

questions.rec_reason: You named the pair yourself, the shared Rin makes the rhyme legal Dawi, and a brother known as Snorin in Common gives Borin's terrible jokes a target at home.

questions.title: A comic name, a grim end
questions.question: When someone with a comic name dies badly, how does the page carry the name?
questions.context: R49-38 lets 'characters whose humour is their voice' be openly funny, and among the Kharven 'The name of the recently dead is not spoken' until given on (R23-11). Abercrombie's Forley the Weakest dies under his name, and the name makes the death worse.

options.label: Straight, as any death
options.consequence: The name is used plainly and nobody remarks on it; the death gets the same clinical weight as any other. The joke was spent while he lived.
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin went with it, under the shafts, under the ice. They had him out inside a minute. Water had frozen in his beard, and his lips were the blue of snow after sundown. The bonesetter worked his chest until her arms shook. Snorin lay on the bank with his eyes half open and did not move again. Somebody fetched a hide-coat to cover him, and the sledge-team stood steaming in the cold.

options.label: The name turns to grief
options.consequence: Someone says the comic name at the death and the joke becomes the wound. Among the Kharven the name then goes unspoken until it is given on (R23-11).
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin went with it, under the shafts, under the ice. They had him out inside a minute, beard frozen solid, lips gone blue. The bonesetter worked his chest until her arms shook. "Snorin," the foreman said, and shook him by the collar. "Snorin. Up. You've slept enough." He went on saying it after the bonesetter had stopped, until the name was only a sound in the cold.

options.label: Gallows wit at the death
options.consequence: The dying man or his comrades make the joke on his name at the death itself, gallows wit from people whose work earns it (R5-D). The laugh and the death share the beat.
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin came out from under the shafts with his chest stove in. He opened one eye at the foreman. "Don't," he said. "Don't you say it." The foreman said it anyway: that a man called Snorin might have had the manners to die in his sleep. Snorin laughed, once, and blood came up with the laugh, black on the snow, and he did not draw the next breath.

options.label: The true name returns
options.consequence: At the death someone says the true name the comic one covered, and the reader hears it for the first time. The joke stays with the living; the true name goes on the roll of the dead.
options.sample: The sledge went through at the ford's edge and Snorin went with it, under the shafts, under the ice. They had him out inside a minute, beard frozen solid, lips gone blue. The bonesetter worked his chest until her arms shook, and then stopped. The foreman knelt in the slush and said the name the Guild form had never carried, Kalrin Torensson, every stop kept hard, the way the holds said it. Nobody else on that bank had known it.

questions.rec_reason: It is the Forley move: the name the column laughed at becomes the one nobody can stop saying, and the laugh that came before makes the death cost more.

questions.title: Places, inns, ships and gear
questions.question: Beyond people, what may carry a comic name?
questions.context: R50-22 gives a place 'several names, one per culture that uses it', and R50-13 lists an item's names 'side by side'. Technique names stay under R50-11's 'two words at most' and R8-22's literal gloss (the name's flat English meaning).

options.label: Inns, taverns and shops
options.consequence: Signboards and their regulars' nicknames carry the joke, in every culture's towns.
options.sample:
The Drowned Gauger: a draw-district alehouse with a gauge-housing for a sign.
The Honest Measure, called the Short Pint: a tavern by the proof-house.
The Second Bowl: a Kharven eating-house, named in the teeth of the proverb.

options.label: Streets and places
options.consequence: The commons' names for streets, fords and districts sit beside the official ones, one per culture (R50-22). The Accord's Latin name stays grave.
options.sample:
Pinchpenny Row: a street of moneylenders, Via Fenoris (street of interest) on the Accord map.
Dead Horse Ford: no horse had died there in living memory.
The Wet Wood: the Kharven name for an Accord barracks that never kept its word.

options.label: Ships, sledges and engines
options.consequence: Crews' names for vessels, sledge-teams, draw-engines and gun-carriages, beside whatever the registry wrote.
options.sample:
Mabel's Mercy: a river dredger, sunk twice and raised twice.
The Widow's Pace: a supply sledge-team never once late or early.
Old Sulk: a draw-engine at a pumping house that would not start in the cold.

options.label: Weapons and items
options.consequence: Weapons and gear take soldiers' folk names beside their true names (R50-13): the true name in the maker's tongue stays grave, and the folk name may joke. Technique names keep R50-11 and R8-22.
options.sample:
Mother's Spoon: a Kharven sergeant's war-axe, which had stirred worse than broth.
The Argument: a Hallenfeld captain's shotgun, which ended them.
The Magistrate's Cough: a proofed fowling piece that settled debts.

questions.rec_reason: Names on things are the commons' humour at its most natural and land on nobody's dignity, and R50-13 and R50-22 already make room for a folk name beside the true one.

questions.title: Who notices the joke
questions.question: Who on the page may notice that a name is funny?
questions.context: R5-C1: 'The narration never winks', with 'No line acknowledging that the reader knows better.' In close third person the narration runs through one character's head, so what he notices is his. Humour 'arrives inside dialogue and narration already in progress' (R5-D).

options.label: Characters aloud only
options.consequence: Narration uses the name like any other, and only speech touches the joke: a character says it, mocks it or pointedly leaves it alone.
options.sample: The inspector came down the conduit stair with her slate under her arm and the Guild seal on a cord at her neck. "Pinchgauge," she said. "From the proof-house." She read the gauge-housing, wrote a figure, and showed it to Marten. It was a hair under the meter. When she had gone back up the stair the stoker spoke into the firebox. "Pinchgauge. And her father before her." Marten fed the fire.

options.label: Close POV may notice
options.consequence: The POV's own head may register the joke in his own idiom, as he would think it. The narrator outside him never remarks, so R5-C1 stands.
options.sample: The inspector came down the conduit stair with her slate under her arm and the Guild seal on a cord at her neck. "Pinchgauge," she said. "From the proof-house." Of course she was. Marten watched her read the gauge-housing and write a figure, and when she showed it him it was a hair under the meter, and he thought her grandfather had likely read light as well, and his grandfather before him.

options.label: Narration may remark once
options.consequence: At first use the narration may note the joke once, dryly, in its own voice. R5-C1 narrows to its core: no line knowing better than the POV about the plot.
options.sample: The inspector came down the conduit stair with her slate under her arm and the Guild seal on a cord at her neck. Her name was Pinchgauge, and in four generations no Pinchgauge had read a meter high. She read the gauge-housing, wrote a figure, and showed it to Marten. It was a hair under. The family had kept its record.

questions.rec_reason: A close POV noticing is a character noticing, so the no-wink law holds and the joke still lands where you read it.

questions.title: Walk-ons with comic names
questions.question: May a one-scene person carry a comic name before he has spoken twice?
questions.context: R50-27: a new person is 'a role (the gate-clerk) until they speak twice or matter'. Pratchett and Dickens name walk-ons at once, often with the joke as the whole character.

options.label: Role first, as now
options.consequence: R50-27 stands: the walk-on is the gate guard until he speaks twice or matters, and then he gets a name, comic or strict.
options.sample: The gate guard at the lower arch let the cart stand in the wind while he read the seal. He held it upside down for a while, then the right way up, and handed it back with a grunt. "Through." The ox leaned into the traces. Above them on the wall someone bawled down about his supper, and the guard bawled back, and the cart rolled under the arch into the smoke of the outer town.

options.label: Comic name on sight
options.consequence: A walk-on may carry a comic name in narration from his first line, the Pratchett move, while strict names still wait on R50-27. A walk-on named for a joke does not die in that scene.
options.sample: Dozy Wat, who kept the lower arch, let the cart stand in the wind while he read the seal. He held it upside down for a while, then the right way up, and handed it back with a grunt. "Through." The ox leaned into the traces. Above them on the wall someone bawled down about his supper, and Dozy Wat bawled back, and the cart rolled under the arch into the smoke of the outer town.

options.label: Nickname in a mouth
options.consequence: A walk-on may be named at once only by a nickname in someone else's mouth; the narration keeps the role until R50-27 is met. A walk-on named for a joke does not die in that scene.
options.sample: The gate guard at the lower arch let the cart stand in the wind while he read the seal. He held it upside down for a while, then the right way up, and handed it back with a grunt. "Through." The ox leaned into the traces. "Dozy!" someone bawled from the wall. "Your broth's gone to ice!" The guard bawled back, and the cart rolled under the arch into the smoke of the outer town.

questions.rec_reason: Nicknames arrive where soldiers and gate crews really make them, in each other's mouths, and the narration's discipline under R50-27 survives intact.

questions.title: How comic names get made
questions.question: How should comic names be produced at the table?
questions.context: R50-30 lets Natalie 'name by ear to keep the pace', with names checked against the banks and sound rules at scene end. R50-18 already makes a name outside every bank a legal outlier, and R50-28 makes a coined word canon 'only if Isaac reuses it'.

options.label: A comic bank per culture
options.consequence: Each Standing Inventory (the per-culture texture file) gains a comic-name list of bynames, nicknames, rhyming sets and signboards, built in that culture's sound rules.
options.sample:
Kharven: Two-Bowls, Short-Stack, Wet Wood, Full Mouth.
Dawi: sets on Rin, Grim and Tor; Twelvecasks; Kurlo.
Accord and Northern: Pinchgauge, Spendlove, Tardipes, Hob and Dob.

options.label: By ear, sound-checked
options.consequence: Natalie coins comic names live; the scene-end check passes each as an outlier (R50-18) so long as it keeps its culture's sound rules, and flags any that break them.
options.sample:
Dozy Wat: coined at a gate, passed.
Snorin: coined at a Guild counter, passed as a Common nickname.
Gripsnack: passed, since goblin sound rules allowed it.

options.label: A floor per crowd scene
options.consequence: Every scene with a crowd, muster, market or tavern carries at least one comic name, checked by verify_scene (the MCP's draft checker). Quiet scenes and two-handers owe none.
options.sample:
A muster at the Seat: Kettle and the Garth twins.
A Guild hall queue: Snorin.
A death-house Waiting: none owed, none used.

options.label: A pitch list per session
options.consequence: At session start Natalie offers five comic names for the scene's culture and you keep the ones you like; kept names join the bank, and the rest are dropped.
options.sample:
Kharven Seat, tonight: Two-Bowls, Kettle, Dozy Wat, Mother Gristle, the Second Bowl.
Kept: Kettle, Mother Gristle.
Dropped: the rest, unused.

questions.rec_reason: A bank gives each culture's comedy its own sound and keeps it fast at the table, and the sound check stops the scene-end pass failing a good joke. A quota or a nightly vote would turn comedy into a chore.

questions.title: How far the naming law bends
questions.question: How far should comic names bend the current naming rows?
questions.context: The rows in play are the banks (R20-3 Dawi, R37-1 Mahuo, R40-1 Moto), the sound rules (R23-11, R23-10), the walk-on rule R50-27 and the scene-end check R50-30. ME1 decides where the new law is written; this decides what in the naming law changes.

options.label: Inside current law
options.consequence: No row is amended. Comic names live as outliers (R50-18), bynames and nicknames, and any answer above that needs more simply lapses.
options.sample:
R50-27: unchanged.
R50-30: unchanged; comic outliers pass under R50-18.
The banks: unchanged.

options.label: Narrow amendments
options.consequence: Only the rows your answers above bend are amended, each in one line naming its answer: R50-30 for the sound check, R50-27 only if NM12 opens walk-ons. Banks and sound rules stand.
options.sample:
R50-30: amended to pass comic outliers on sound rules alone.
R50-27: amended only if NM12 is B.
The banks: unchanged.

options.label: Banks gain comic slots
options.consequence: B, plus each culture's naming rows gain a comic-names clause pointing to that culture's comic bank in its Standing Inventory, so load_rules serves the bank with the law.
options.sample:
R20-3 (Dawi): gains rhyme sets on a shared element and a byname list.
R23-2 (Northern): gains talking surnames and pet-name pairs.
R23-11 (Far-Northern): gains scarcity bynames and cheap names.

options.label: Comic names exempt
options.consequence: Comic names are exempt from every bank and sound rule (R20-3, R23-11, R40-1) and are checked only for real grammar (R50-01). The banks govern strict names alone.
options.sample:
Snorin as a Dawi given name: legal.
A comic given name for a new Moto cadet: legal.
Any pun: checked for real grammar only.

questions.rec_reason: It matches a comic bank per culture (NM13) and keeps the comedy inside each people's own sound, so the jokes read as the world's habit and the strict names keep their weight.

sections.title: Explicit scenes under the blend
sections.intro: Two questions. R49-51's plain, crude naming stays the floor; these ask what the Eastern traditions add to it, and where.

questions.title: Eastern techniques beside clinical specificity
questions.question: Which Eastern techniques may join the plain, clinical specificity of an explicit scene?
questions.context: This reopens R49-51, ruled 2026-09-26: explicit narration stays 'plain and crude', 'blunt in naming'; table rule 9 tracks positions and commits onomatopoeia. Japanese and Chinese erotic writing works through season and nature imagery, restraint and the unsaid, and the morning-after poem of the Heian court (Japan's classical court); Japanese gitaigo are mimetic words for textures and states that make no sound.

options.label: Season and nature imagery
options.consequence: An explicit scene may set a season or nature image beside the anatomy (frost, snow, blossom, the brazier), carrying mood without replacing the plain words.
options.sample: Frost had grown ferns across the inside of the shutter, and the brazier had burned down to one red eye in the ash. Sae lay back on the quilts and drew Toma down by the hips, and he went into her slowly, the cold of the room on his back and the heat of her cunt close round his cock. Outside, a long slide of snow went off the eaves. She hooked a heel behind his thigh. Where their breath reached the shutter the ferns blurred, and ran.

options.label: Held detail at the peak
options.consequence: At chosen moments, usually the peak, one held physical detail may carry the beat; plain specificity governs the rest, and the aftermath is still written.
options.sample: Sae lay back on the quilts and drew Toma down by the hips, and he went into her slowly, the cold of the room on his back and the heat of her cunt close round his cock. She set the pace with a heel hooked behind his thigh. He let her. When it came for her she reached past his head and closed her hand on the brazier's iron rim. It was hot. She held on. Afterward there were two red lines across her palm, and she would not let him dress them.

options.label: The poem after
options.consequence: An explicit scene may close on a written or spoken exchange (a morning poem, a note, a line answered) as part of its aftermath beat.
options.sample:
Toma had gone into her slowly, the cold of the room on his back, and Sae had held him there with a heel behind his thigh until neither of them could keep quiet. Afterward he slept. She rose in the grey before the Bow, knelt at the low table, and wrote on the back of a ration slip in her small house hand:

*The brazier is ash. Still the quilts
hold a heat that is not the fire's.*

She left it under his cup and went out to weigh the bread.

options.label: Mimetic words
options.consequence: Mimetic words for texture and state (the Japanese gitaigo habit, and each culture's own) join table rule 9's onomatopoeia, romanised and never italic.
options.sample: Sae lay back on the quilts and drew Toma down by the hips, and he went into her slowly, nuru-nuru, slick and close, the cold of the room on his back. She set the pace with a heel behind his thigh. The quilts hissed under them, shu, shu. Her breath came in small catches against his throat. When she came she pulled him in hard and held, and her whole body went biku-biku round him, again and again, until it let go.

questions.rec_reason: Image, the held detail and the morning poem each add what the Eastern tradition does best without taking the blunt words away. RH4's few Inventory sound words still reach an explicit scene as they reach any other; D's stacked texture mimetics (the sample's nuru-nuru) read as comic-book effects in English and would undercut the plain register.

questions.title: Keyed to culture or free
questions.question: Are the Eastern explicit techniques keyed to culture, or free in any scene?
questions.context: R49-51 sets one register for every culture. The Moto court and Eresse carry courtly restraint in their Inventories and voices; Kharven, Dawi and the Northern English run blunt. Keying keeps cultures distinct in bed as everywhere else; freeing the techniques gives every scene the whole kit.

options.label: Free in any scene
options.consequence: The techniques chosen in XS1 are open to every explicit scene, whatever the cultures in the room.

options.label: Keyed to the culture
options.consequence: Courtly cultures (the Moto court, Eresse, the Mahuo houses, the lineage halls) take the XS1 techniques; Kharven, Dawi, Accord and Northern scenes stay plain, crude and clinical.

options.label: Keyed to the POV
options.consequence: The POV's culture decides: a Moto POV writes with image and the held detail, a Kharven POV blunt, whoever the lover is; the lover's culture shows in what they do and say.

questions.rec_reason: It follows WOTR's POV discipline: narration sees through its viewpoint, so a scene between two cultures carries both, one in the prose and one in the body of the other person.

sections.title: Method and output
sections.intro: How your answers become law: where the rulings live, which general checks verify_scene gains, what happens to the archived scenes, and the order of work. The vocabulary checks are VB13 and the range check is DD7.

questions.title: Where the new law lives
questions.question: How do your answers land in the repo and in Natalie's standing prompt?
questions.context: Rulings enter the index through log_ruling as dated rule rows. NATALIE.md still calls WOTR an 'Eastern skeleton' under 'Western flesh' and names Martin, Tolkien and Abercrombie; R5-A-FLESH_CHANGES says the same in law. Most companion guides are 2026-09-12 editions, older than the 09-26 law, and the Master Style Directive still bans status screens.

options.label: Rule doc and NATALIE rewrite
options.consequence: One dated Style Law doc logged through log_ruling; NATALIE.md's models line and Prose Standards rewritten to it; R5-A-FLESH_CHANGES, R5-E-MARTIN_WINS_RULING and R11-1 superseded or amended as K1 decides.

options.label: Rule doc only
options.consequence: The rule doc is logged and served by load_rules; NATALIE.md gains only a pointer, so its 'Western flesh' line and older craft lines stay until a later pass.

options.label: A, plus new guide editions
options.consequence: A, then new editions of the Master Style Directive, Combat Craft Guide, Dialogue Craft Standards and Scene Writing Process Guide, so no companion document still teaches the old law.

questions.rec_reason: Natalie reads NATALIE.md and the guides every session; if any of them still teaches 'Western flesh' or bans status screens, the old law keeps writing scenes after the new one is logged.

questions.title: New checks in verify_scene
questions.question: Which new verify_scene checks should come with the law?
questions.context: verify_scene fails dashes, antithesis and the hard-ban words and warns on rhythm; with --combat it warns on a fight with no HEMA term, though its list includes cut, guard and point, so it seldom fires. It already leaves '>' quote blocks and '|' tables out of the rhythm counts but reads verse set any other way (italic lines, verse in speech) as prose, and knows no honorifics and no translated web-novel formulas.

options.label: Combat words by school
options.consequence: verify --combat takes a school (blade, japanese, chinese, korean, percussion) or reads the culture tag, and warns only when a fight carries none of that school's terms.

options.label: A verse marker
options.consequence: A marked verse block (a poem, a lament, a declaration in lines) is left out of the rhythm statistics and word count; the dash and hard-ban checks still read it.

options.label: Address check
options.consequence: A WARN when a speaker uses another stratum's honorifics, or when narration carries a suffix in a scene whose POV culture has none.

options.label: Stock-formula watch
options.consequence: A WARN on translated web-novel formulas (you court death, this junior, this old man, lose face) in narration, and an info line in speech, so the flavour stays where DL2 puts it.

questions.rec_reason: The school lists and the verse marker stop the checker fighting the blend, and the formula watch keeps translated stock phrases out of narration under any DL2 answer; an address check would misfire in every mixed room.

questions.title: The archived scenes
questions.question: What happens to the scenes archived under the old law?
questions.context: scenes/MANIFEST.md lists 160 archived files written under 'Western flesh', a few still carrying em dashes and Büri-era names. Archived scenes are canon of their day, and scene_recall and the drafting tools read them as precedent, so old style can leak forward if nothing marks it.

options.label: Leave them as written
options.consequence: The archive stays untouched; the new law governs what is written from now on.

options.label: Leave them, tag the edition
options.consequence: The archive stays untouched, and scenes/MANIFEST.md gains a law-edition column so the drafting tools and scene_recall stop treating old style as precedent.

options.label: Revise the live threads
options.consequence: Scenes in the live threads are revised to the new law, prose only, with events and Isaac's lines unchanged; the rest stay as written.

options.label: Revise everything
options.consequence: Every archived scene is revised to the new law, events and Isaac's lines unchanged: a large pass across about 160 files.

questions.rec_reason: The scenes stay true to what was played, and the tag stops the old style teaching new drafts, at almost no cost.

questions.title: Proof and the order of work
questions.question: In what order does the work run, and is the law proved on a test scene before it binds?
questions.context: The law can bind at once and be proved by the next real turn, be tried first on a test scene in a live thread, or ship with a bank of sample passages per culture showing the blend. No such bank exists yet; this questionnaire's samples are the nearest thing.

options.label: Law, test scene, then bank
options.consequence: The law is logged live; one test scene in a live thread follows; anything that reads wrong becomes a dated amendment; then a sample bank for Kharven, Moto, Accord, the Mahuo and the lineage halls.

options.label: Test scene first
options.consequence: The law stays a draft until a test scene written under it has been read; then it is logged and the bank built from what the test showed.

options.label: Law and bank together
options.consequence: The law is logged with a sample bank of five beats per live-thread culture (fight, council, quiet, explicit, system moment), and the bank serves as the proof.

options.label: Law only
options.consequence: The law is logged and binds at once; the next real turn is the test, and no sample bank is written.

questions.rec_reason: It puts the law to work at once, catches what reads wrong in a real scene, and builds the bank from a law that has already been tested.

settled.point: Unreliable narration: whether the POV's narration may be wrong
settled.why_not_asked: Live law already allows it: close narration 'can be wrong the way the character is wrong', the POV's reflection 'may be wrong', and Table Rule 8 keeps lies uncorrected. Every blend option keeps this.

settled.point: Psychic distance per POV
settled.why_not_asked: Each POV's distance is set by its register and by the 2026-09-26 lift toward deep. The blend's wide shots are asked in VO2 and the storyteller in VO1; neither moves the per-POV bands.

settled.point: Free indirect discourse (narration in the POV's own idiom, verdicts included)
settled.why_not_asked: Legal in every option, and the house's present-tense laws of the world inside past narration rest on it.

settled.point: Tense: present for roleplay turns, past for written scenes and books
settled.why_not_asked: Isaac ruled it by job on 2026-09-26 and no tradition in the blend argues against it. A readout keeps its own form whatever the tense around it (LR3, LR4).

settled.point: Memory flashbacks inside a scene
settled.why_not_asked: Full flashbacks of a page or more are already legal. A flashback into an opponent's past mid-fight breaks the POV lock, which VO2 covers, and is a combat device, which the CB section covers.

settled.point: Turn and set-piece length
settled.why_not_asked: Isaac set these numbers himself on 2026-09-26 (about 3,500 words a turn, 5,000+ for a set piece); the blend changes how the words are spent, not how many. The book pipeline's 3,500-word chapter already sits near web-serial length.

settled.point: The chapter as a hard unit with one objective and a hook, opening inside the situation
settled.why_not_asked: This is already a light-novel inheritance kept in law, and it suits web-serial and LitRPG chapters as it stands. SP4 widens the kinds of hook.

settled.point: Marking a real jump in time or place
settled.why_not_asked: A blank line or ornament is already allowed; every tradition in the blend uses the same device.

settled.point: How often italic thought appears, and NPC thoughts in roleplay turns
settled.why_not_asked: Italic thought 'appears often' and roleplay keeps one thought per NPC; both already fit light-novel and LitRPG interiority. Lock breaks in written scenes are asked in VO2.

settled.point: High mythic style and full elegy in narration
settled.why_not_asked: Already free whenever the moment calls for it, which covers the war tales' lament and pansori's slow cadence as well as Tolkien.

settled.point: Anaphora and the triad
settled.why_not_asked: Repeated openings and three-part lists are legal everywhere; RH1 asks only about matched pairs and the long chain, which the run rule and landing rule still catch.

settled.point: Unbound as the model for stat talk in a mouth
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-12 in Isaac's words, 'like how people talk about stats in LitRPGs like Unbound'; K6 asks only which works join it.

settled.point: The anti-machine bans: dashes, not-X-but-Y, the Ladder, the hard-ban words
settled.why_not_asked: These catch machine-written prose and are neutral between traditions (R15-1: 'about prose failing, not about period'); every option in this group keeps them.

settled.point: Isaac's characters are never thought, voiced or acted for
settled.why_not_asked: Standing law for every job; any first-person or interiority option here applies to NPCs and Natalie's POVs only, and Isaac overrules any thought in his own character's head.

settled.point: Every outdoor scene shows the actual weather, tracked like a clock.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law already requires it, and every landscape option above builds on it.

settled.point: Every beat carries at least one detail that could only exist in this world.
settled.why_not_asked: Every tradition in the blend agrees with it; it is the floor any range rule stands on. DD2 and DD6 decide only where the larger passages sit.

settled.point: A mixed room layers every culture present in roughly equal measure.
settled.why_not_asked: Culture-keyed noticing (DS5) works inside it; the blend gives no reason to change the measure.

settled.point: World facts are looked up and gaps flagged; a culture with no Inventory gets one drafted from the wiki before its scene.
settled.why_not_asked: New Inventory fields (DS6) and the missing Mahuo, Hon-guk, lineage-hall, chartered-household and tundra Inventories are drafted under these rules as each culture reaches the page.

settled.point: Texture invented in play is canon once logged.
settled.why_not_asked: Wider description needs exactly this licence, and it already stands.

settled.point: Wear, rust, weathering and labour are described in full.
settled.why_not_asked: It agrees with wabi-sabi and with the Victorian eye alike; DS7 builds on it.

settled.point: Travel and waiting pass in a line when nothing is at stake.
settled.why_not_asked: The range rules govern what is on the page; skipping dull stretches stays, and a route described in full (DS9) is for roads that matter.

settled.point: Real history is taken exactly and bent one step, and real cultures may be blended into one WOTR culture.
settled.why_not_asked: These already license Eastern and Western subjects alike in every Inventory.

settled.point: Prices on the page are quoted from the approved price table.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law decides it and the table is approved; how price, grade and provenance reach the prose is DS12, and the set-off item card is LR17.

settled.point: A person's first-sight inventory lands all at once, in one descriptive passage.
settled.why_not_asked: You ruled exactly this on 2026-09-26, and the blend backs it: the Victorian portrait, the cultivation appearance paragraph and the war-tale armour list all land at once. DD3 and DD4 ask who gets one and in what order.

settled.point: A 3,500-word turn is filled about half texture and talk, half the world moving.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law decides the split; where a turn's description sits is DD2, and whether turns take the blend lighter than books is K8.

settled.point: Every working costs something visible in the body.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law decides it, and cultivation and LitRPG both price power too, so the blend gives no reason to reopen it.

settled.point: No figure on the page is invented.
settled.why_not_asked: Absolute in law; the form numbers take on the page is asked in LR.

settled.point: Stat names, Grades, Stages and EU figures in narration.
settled.why_not_asked: Already free since 2026-09-26; screens and frequency are asked in LR. NATALIE.md's Magic Frame line ('names only in a mouth...') is stale and should be rewritten to match.

settled.point: The three-layer account (Aether, Wellspring, Essence) at a working's first display and finisher.
settled.why_not_asked: It governs how much mechanism appears, which the blend does not change; MY asks only how that mechanism reads.

settled.point: A faculty as the grammatical subject (the Eastern eye-technique convention).
settled.why_not_asked: R54-21 already allows it inside a close register; R6-2 is the older row and should be marked as narrowed by it.

settled.point: Real idea-names from Earth's traditions in scenes.
settled.why_not_asked: Already legal anywhere they fit; MY1 asks only whether cultivation words become a school's own lens.

settled.point: Elegy attaches to a named concrete thing that is gone.
settled.why_not_asked: Mono no aware (the gentle sadness of passing things) and han (Korean grief held without release) already fit it; the Gone lists supply the objects.

settled.point: Chants appear in their own language.
settled.why_not_asked: DT6 covers verse; chants stay as ruled.

settled.point: Similes have no rate; only two competing over one beat are flagged.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law already allows the long comparison from the POV's life; DT8 asks only whether the epic simile may reach beyond it.

settled.point: Folk beliefs about magic stand uncorrected by the narration.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law, and it suits every option in MY8; commoners keep their folk words whatever the register.

settled.point: Technique names spoken aloud in a fight (the named attack).
settled.why_not_asked: R8-24 and R50-09 (2026-09-26) already let an art be called as often as a beat allows, each call costing the beat, and R8-23 names techniques every time they are used, so the shōnen named attack is law; an onlooker naming the form is R12-4's knowing second. R8-26-ONE_RELEASE_PER_SCENE is stale and should be marked superseded by R50-09. MY9 asks only what form a name takes on the page.

settled.point: Ornate against spare description (the Mishima end against the Gu Long end).
settled.why_not_asked: Ornate figuration is already legal by ear (high mythic style, stacked adjectives, extended and stacked metaphor). The spare end is DD1's density and RH2's paragraphing, and bending the rhythm caps for a long passage is RH1.

settled.point: McCarthy's and-chain (clauses strung on 'and').
settled.why_not_asked: Already the house habit outside a beat; whether long cumulative sentences may run at a beat is asked in RH1.

settled.point: How a landscape view is composed (shanshui planes, far to near, against the Western route).
settled.why_not_asked: Asked in DS9 (the wide view in far, middle and near planes, and land as route), with SP3 for far-to-near openings and VO2 for sweeps.

settled.point: Sound words and mimetic words outside explicit scenes.
settled.why_not_asked: Asked in RH4.

settled.point: The measured pause (ma) and the cut before the emotional payoff.
settled.why_not_asked: Asked in SP2 (stillness written long) and SP4 (breaking off before the payoff).

settled.point: How a Stage breakthrough is written.
settled.why_not_asked: Asked in LR23, with LR14 for how the new Stage is confirmed.

settled.point: Appraising an object of power: grade, maker, history and price in prose.
settled.why_not_asked: Asked in DS12 (appraisal and lineage in prose) and LR17 (the item card).

settled.point: Dashes in speech, including the manga cut-off shout
settled.why_not_asked: The dash ban targets failing prose in every culture and period; a shout cut off mid-word stays an ellipsis.

settled.point: The clinical floor for wounds and exchanges
settled.why_not_asked: Every combat option keeps full clinical gore and the exchange floor; the blend only adds rites, images and shapes around them (CB3, CB6).

settled.point: Death is permanent
settled.why_not_asked: The rival bond and the mid-fight flashback both work inside it, so nothing in the blend needs it reopened.

settled.point: Japonic honorifics in speech
settled.why_not_asked: Already law; DL1 asks only about the Korean and Chinese strata, NE2 about narration.

settled.point: Name order and how a character is first named
settled.why_not_asked: Korean family name first and introduction by the name the POV would use are already law and suit any blend.

settled.point: Nobody translates their own technique aloud
settled.why_not_asked: The opponent's contempt-as-instruction voice already carries the shōnen habit of explaining a technique mid-fight.

settled.point: Fragment antithesis ('Not regret. Recognition.')
